title: Machine learning foundations
lead: What learning from data is, written out as mathematics you can compute: a model, a loss derived from a noise model, an optimiser whose behaviour an eigenvalue predicts, and the habit that separates a model that works from one that only looks as if it does, which is evaluating it honestly.
prerequisites: No earlier module: this is the first module of the series.
Calculus: partial derivatives, the chain rule and the gradient of a function of several variables.
Linear algebra: matrix products and transposes, inverse and rank, eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix, and orthogonality (the SVD is introduced where it is used).
Probability: random variables, expectation, variance and independence (Section 5 opens with a refresher on the Gaussian, Laplace, Bernoulli and categorical distributions).
Python: functions, loops and NumPy arrays; no experience of a machine-learning library is assumed.
outcomes: State any learning method as its five ingredients (data, model, loss, optimiser, evaluation) and name the assumption each one carries.
Derive the gradient and the normal equations of least squares, and explain the solution as an orthogonal projection onto the column space of $\mathbf{X}$.

Predict from the Hessian's eigenvalues whether gradient descent converges at a given learning rate ($\eta < 2/\lambda_{\max}$) and roughly how many steps it needs (in proportion to $\kappa$), and repair a stalled run by centring and standardising the features.

Derive squared error, absolute error and cross-entropy as negative log-likelihoods, and ridge and lasso as MAP estimates under Gaussian and Laplace priors, with $\lambda = \sigma^2/(N\tau^2)$ for ridge.
Derive the gradients of logistic and softmax regression, implement logistic regression in NumPy and check it against scikit-learn.
Derive the bias–variance decomposition and use validation curves, learning curves and $k$-fold cross-validation to choose model capacity and regularisation strength.

Design an evaluation free of the common leaks (preprocessing fitted inside the folds, group- and time-aware splits, nested selection, a test set opened once), attach a standard error or bootstrap interval to every reported number, and compare two models on one test set with a paired bootstrap and McNemar's exact test.

Choose and compute the metric a decision needs (precision, recall, F1, ROC AUC, average precision, expected calibration error, Brier score), including the effect of the base rate and a cost-based threshold.

Fit a physical model by weighted and nonlinear least squares, read its normalised residuals and $\chi^2_\nu$, quantify the uncertainty of its parameters and state the range outside which its predictions are unsupported.
Say what $k$-NN, decision trees, random forests, gradient boosting, kernel methods and SVMs, Gaussian processes, $k$-means and PCA do, and which to try first as a baseline.
software: scikit-learn, using only its built-in datasets (`load_breast_cancer`, `load_diabetes`, `make_friedman1`, `make_moons`), so nothing is downloaded.
Jupyter or any Python REPL (optional); Google Colab is a free alternative, and no GPU is needed.
PyTorch is not used in this module; it enters in Module 02.

sections.title: The learning problem
sections.purpose: State what learning from data is as five explicit choices, fix the notation for the series, and introduce the running examples of this module.
must_cover: The two motivating engineering functions from the source, kept: the sag of a scaffold as a function of material and geometry (a solver exists but took a person-year to build) and the probability that a hazard is controllable (no theory; estimated by people). Learning is obtaining such a function from examples when examples are cheaper than theory.

Formal set-up: unknown f*, data distribution P over (x, y), sample D = {(x_i, y_i)}, i = 1..N, drawn from P. The goal is good prediction on inputs not yet seen; predicting the examples already held is a lookup table.

Expected risk R(f) = E_(x,y)~P [ℓ(f(x), y)] against empirical risk L(θ) = (1/N) Σ_i ℓ(f_θ(x_i), y_i). Write both; the gap between them is the subject of Sections 8 and 10. The training loss is biased low because the optimiser chose θ to make it small.

Three settings: supervised (regression when y is continuous, classification when y is one of K labels), unsupervised (structure without y: k-means and PCA in Section 11, neural forms in Module 05), reinforcement learning (a reward after actions; Module 09 uses it to train language models).

The five ingredients, each with the reason it matters: data (and the distribution P it came from — the one people forget); model f_θ (hypothesis class; a line has two parameters, a language model billions); loss ℓ ≥ 0 and the empirical risk; optimiser (almost always a variant of gradient descent); evaluation on data the model was not fitted to. A method you cannot state this way is one you do not understand yet.

Inputs as numbers: the feature vector x ∈ R^d. Categories are one-hot encoded (a K-way category becomes K binary columns), never coded as integers, which impose an order and equal spacing; the exception is a genuinely ordinal scale, and even then integer codes assume equal steps. Then one sentence on learned embeddings: a one-hot vector times a trainable K × m table picks out one row of the table, so an embedding is such a table learned with the rest of the model, and it works the same way for any categorical feature (a part number, a supplier, a sensor ID) as for the tokens of a language model. Link Module 06, Section 4, where the token embedding enters the residual stream (Module 06, Section 11 counts its V × d table); do not say that Module 06 covers embeddings of other categorical features, because it does not.

A map of the module's running examples so readers recognise them: the synthetic regression with N = 200, d = 3 (Sections 2–4, Lab 1); noisy samples of sin(2πx) (Sections 8–9, Lab 3); the breast-cancer classifier (Sections 6–7, Labs 2 and 4); the hyperelastic compression test (Sections 5 and 12, Lab 5).
worked_examples: The five ingredients written out side by side for two methods at the ends of the range. (a) This module's regression: data 200 rows, 3 features, Gaussian noise of standard deviation 0.1; model w·x + b with 4 parameters; loss squared error; optimiser normal equations or gradient descent; evaluation RMSE on held-out rows. (b) The language model of the hypothetical case study in Modules 07–10 (about 9.5 billion parameters): data trillions of tokens of text; model a transformer; loss cross-entropy over the vocabulary at every position; optimiser AdamW; evaluation held-out perplexity and task benchmarks. Same five slots, more than nine orders of magnitude apart in parameter count (4 against about 9.5 billion).

The hyperelastic fit of Section 12 in the same table: data 16 (stretch, stress, uncertainty) triples from one compression test, P = specimens of this gel tested this way; model P = 2c1(λ − λ⁻²), one parameter; loss weighted squared error; optimiser a closed form; evaluation residuals on held-out strain ranges. Flag that the evaluation slot is where the extrapolation question of Section 12 lives.

checks: Why is the training loss not a measure of how good the model is? -> The optimiser chose θ to make it small, so it is biased low; only data not used in fitting estimates the expected risk.

A defect severity {minor, major, critical} is coded 1, 2, 3 in a linear model. What does that assume, and when is it acceptable? -> An order, which is real here, and equal steps: 'major' has an effect exactly halfway between the other two. Keep the integer code only if equal steps are plausible or validation supports them; otherwise one-hot encode, which keeps no order and assumes no spacing. (Exercise e2 takes the unordered case.)

sections.title: Least squares and its geometry
sections.purpose: Fit linear regression in closed form, read the solution as an orthogonal projection, and know when the problem is ill-posed and how to compute it stably.
must_cover: Set-up: f(x) = w·x + b; absorb b by appending a constant 1, so X ∈ R^(N×(d+1)) has rows x_i and y ∈ R^N. Loss L(w) = (1/N)‖Xw − y‖².

Gradient derived, not asserted: expand ‖Xw − y‖² = wᵀXᵀXw − 2yᵀXw + yᵀy; use ∇(wᵀAw) = 2Aw for symmetric A and ∇(bᵀw) = b; obtain ∇L = (2/N)Xᵀ(Xw − y). Hessian (2/N)XᵀX is positive semidefinite because vᵀXᵀXv = ‖Xv‖² ≥ 0, so L is convex.
Normal equations XᵀXw = Xᵀy and w* = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy when X has full column rank (needs at least d + 1 linearly independent rows).

Geometry: ŷ = Xw* is the orthogonal projection of y onto the column space of X; the residual r = y − ŷ satisfies Xᵀr = 0, which is what 'normal' (perpendicular) means. Hat matrix H = X(XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀ is symmetric and idempotent (H² = H) with trace d + 1. With an intercept column the residuals sum to zero. Pythagoras on centred vectors: total sum of squares = explained + residual, which defines R² (used again in Section 7).

Rank deficiency: duplicated or affinely dependent columns (temperature in °C next to °F with an intercept; all K one-hot columns plus an intercept) make XᵀX singular. Infinitely many w give the same ŷ; the pseudo-inverse X⁺y picks the minimum-norm one. Ridge (Section 9) also removes the ambiguity.

Computation: never form the inverse. Options: Cholesky of XᵀX (fast, but κ(XᵀX) = κ(X)², so it squares the condition number); QR of X (solve Rw = Qᵀy, conditioning κ(X)); SVD X = UΣVᵀ, w = VΣ⁻¹Uᵀy, which also exposes the conditioning through the singular values. np.linalg.lstsq uses an SVD-based LAPACK driver. Cost about Nd² for forming XᵀX or a QR.

The source's NumPy example (N = 200, d = 3, w = (1.5, −2.0, 0.5), b = 0.7, noise 0.1·N(0,1), default_rng(0)) reproduced exactly, and the irreducible error: the residual RMS equals the noise level; a model that fits below it is fitting noise.
worked_examples: Collinearity: add a third column 2x. XᵀX becomes singular (determinant 0). Predictions are unchanged at (1.1, 2.2, 3.3, 4.4); the weights on x and 2x are any (a, c) with a + 2c = 1.1; lstsq returns the minimum-norm pair (0.22, 0.44) with intercept 1.1.

The source code's output: closed form and 500 steps of gradient descent at η = 0.1 both print [1.491, −2.010, 0.505, 0.696]; residual RMS 0.1000 and the unbiased estimate sqrt(RSS/(N − 4)) = 0.1010 — the noise level, recovered.

The four-point fit: points (0,1), (1,3), (2,2), (3,5); the line y = 1.1 + 1.1x; vertical residual segments labelled −0.1, +0.8, −1.3, +0.6; legend shows R² = 0.691.

checks: Why are they called the normal equations? -> They say Xᵀ(y − Xw) = 0: the residual is normal (perpendicular) to every column of X.

You add temperature in °F next to temperature in °C, with an intercept. What happens to XᵀX and to the predictions? -> XᵀX becomes singular because °F = 1.8·°C + 32·(intercept column); the weights are no longer unique, but the projection ŷ, and so the predictions, are unchanged.
Why prefer QR or the SVD to solving XᵀXw = Xᵀy by Cholesky? -> Forming XᵀX squares the condition number; QR and the SVD work with X directly.

sections.title: Gradient descent on a quadratic
sections.purpose: Derive exactly when and how fast gradient descent converges on the least-squares loss, so that learning rate, conditioning and feature scaling become numbers rather than folklore.
must_cover: Why iterate when a closed form exists, and when not to: the solve costs about Nd² + d³ and needs all the data in memory; a gradient step costs about Nd; every model from Module 02 on has no closed form. State the rule of thumb once: small d, use lstsq; large N or d, or streaming data, use the SGD of Section 4; ill-conditioned, rescale first (below).

Exact quadratic form and the error recursion: using the normal equations, L(w) = L(w*) + ½(w − w*)ᵀH(w − w*) with H = (2/N)XᵀX (show the expansion). With e_t = w_t − w*, the update w ← w − η∇L gives e_(t+1) = (I − ηH)e_t. Diagonalise H = QΛQᵀ; in eigen-coordinates each component evolves alone, ẽ_(i,t) = (1 − ηλ_i)^t ẽ_(i,0).

Stability derived: convergence needs |1 − ηλ_i| < 1 for every i, i.e. 0 < η < 2/λ_max. Regimes: η < 1/λ_max monotone; η = 1/λ_max solves the steepest mode in one step; 1/λ_max < η < 2/λ_max the steep mode's factor is negative, so the iterate zig-zags across the valley; η = 2/λ_max neither grows nor decays; η > 2/λ_max diverges geometrically.

Rate: the flattest mode limits speed at factor 1 − ηλ_min. The best fixed step η* = 2/(λ_max + λ_min) equalises the extreme factors and gives ρ = (κ − 1)/(κ + 1) with κ = λ_max/λ_min. Steps to shrink the error by ε: t = ln(1/ε)/(−ln ρ) ≈ (κ/2)ln(1/ε) for large κ; the loss shrinks as ρ^(2t).

Conditioning comes from the features: for centred, uncorrelated features with standard deviations s_j, (1/N)XᵀX = diag(s_j²) and κ = (s_max/s_min)². Uncentred features couple to the intercept: a feature with mean 100 and standard deviation 1 next to the constant column gives (1/N)XᵀX = [[1, 100], [100, 10001]], eigenvalues 10002 and 1.0×10⁻⁴, κ ≈ 1.0×10⁸ — centring alone fixes it. Correlation also inflates κ: two standardised features with correlation ρ have eigenvalues 1 ± ρ and κ = (1 + ρ)/(1 − ρ), so 0.9 gives 19 and 0.99 gives 199; standardisation fixes units, not correlation. The source's units example, made explicit: a span length in millimetres with standard deviation 1000 mm next to a modulus in gigapascals with standard deviation 0.001 GPa (1 MPa batch scatter) — ratio 10⁶, κ = 10¹², and at the best fixed step about (κ/2)ln(10⁶) ≈ 6.9×10¹² iterations for six digits; after standardisation κ ≈ 1.

Standardisation x′ = (x − μ)/s with μ and s from the training set only, applied unchanged to validation and test data (leakage in miniature otherwise; Section 10). Map weights back to original units: w_j = w′_j/s_j, b = b′ − Σ_j μ_j w′_j/s_j.

Beyond quadratics, in two sentences: near any smooth minimum the loss is approximately quadratic with H the Hessian, so η < 2/λ_max(H) governs local stability in Module 02's networks too. For logistic regression the bound computed from the worst-case curvature is sufficient but not necessary (Section 6 and Lab 2's extension).
worked_examples: H = diag(1, 10), κ = 10: η_max = 0.2. At η = 0.1 the factors are 0.9 and 0.0 — the steep mode is solved in one step and the flat mode needs ln(10⁶)/(−ln 0.9) = 131.1, so 132 steps for a 10⁶ error reduction. At η = 0.18 the factors are 0.82 and −0.80 (zig-zag): 69.6, so 70 steps. At η* = 2/11 = 0.182 both factors are ±0.818: 68.8, so 69 steps. At η = 0.21 the steep factor is −1.1 and that component grows 1.1⁵⁰ = 117 times in 50 steps.

Lab 1's data: H has eigenvalues 1.711, 1.922, 2.126, 2.207, so κ = 1.29, η_max = 0.906 and η* = 0.511. GD needs 76 steps at η = 0.1 and 7 at η* to bring ‖w − w*‖ below 10⁻⁶. Multiplying one feature by 1000 and shifting another by 100 gives κ = 1.0×10¹⁰ (scale alone 1.1×10⁶, offset alone 1.0×10⁸) and η_max = 9.7×10⁻⁷; 100,000 steps at 0.9η_max leave the training MSE at 4.28 against 0.0100 achievable. Standardised: κ = 1.22, converged in 6 steps.

checks: With H = diag(2, 200), what is the largest stable learning rate, and which coordinate limits the speed? -> η < 2/200 = 0.01; the λ = 2 coordinate then shrinks by only 1 − 0.02 = 0.98 per step (κ = 100).

sections.title: Stochastic and mini-batch gradient descent
sections.purpose: Explain batch, stochastic and mini-batch gradient descent, derive the noise floor that a constant step leaves, and give a practical procedure for choosing the learning rate.
must_cover: The mini-batch update θ ← θ − η(1/B)Σ_(i∈B)∇ℓ_i. With uniform sampling the mini-batch gradient is unbiased, E[g_B] = ∇L, and its covariance is Σ_g/B (derive from independence for sampling with replacement; without replacement it is slightly smaller).

An epoch is ⌈N/B⌉ updates rather than one, which is why SGD wins on large data; cost per update about Bd. Shuffle each epoch; fix seeds; typical B from 32 to a few thousand; language models use millions of tokens per batch (Module 08).

The noise floor, derived on a 1-D quadratic with curvature λ and gradient-noise variance s²: θ_(t+1) − θ* = (1 − ηλ)(θ_t − θ*) − ηξ_t with Var ξ = s²/B. The stationary variance V satisfies V = (1 − ηλ)²V + η²s²/B, so V = ηs²/(Bλ(2 − ηλ)) ≈ ηs²/(2Bλ). A constant step does not converge; it hovers, with an excess loss ½λV proportional to η/B.

Consequences: decay the step (Robbins–Monro conditions Σ_t η_t = ∞ and Σ_t η_t² < ∞, for example η_t = η₀/(1 + t/τ)) or enlarge the batch. Return to the gd-quadratic widget and raise its gradient-noise slider: the loss flattens at the predicted floor, and halving η halves it.

Choosing η in practice: when the curvature is known, start from 2/λ_max; otherwise run a short log-spaced sweep (for example 10⁻⁴ to 1 in factors of about 3), take the largest η whose loss falls smoothly, then decay. Read the loss curve: rising or NaN means too large; a straight but shallow line on a log plot means too small; a noisy plateau means decay. The learning-rate range test, momentum, Adam and schedules in depth are Module 02's.
Noise as a regulariser: small batches tend to find flatter minima that generalise better — an empirical observation with a partial theory (Keskar et al. 2017). State it with that hedge.

Non-convex models: gradient descent finds a local minimum or a saddle with no guarantee of the best; for large networks the minima found are usually good enough and the difficulty lies in conditioning, initialisation and the learning rate (Module 02).
worked_examples: Updates per epoch: N = 50,000, B = 64 gives ⌈781.25⌉ = 782 updates (the last batch holds 16 examples); 20 epochs are 15,640 updates; full-batch gradient descent makes 20.

The floor in numbers (λ = 1, s² = 1): B = 1, η = 0.1 gives V = 0.1/1.9 = 0.0526 and excess loss 0.0263; η = 0.01 gives V = 0.00503 (excess 0.00251); B = 10 at η = 0.1 gives V = 0.00526. A tenfold smaller step or a tenfold larger batch buys about a tenfold lower floor. (A 400,000-step simulation gives V = 0.0526.)

Lab 1's measurements, averaged over the second half of 50 epochs, against the prediction Σ_i ηs²λ_i/(B(2 − ηλ_i)) with s² = 0.0100: B = 32, η = 0.1: 1.0×10⁻⁴ measured, 1.4×10⁻⁴ predicted; B = 10: 3.1×10⁻⁴ vs 4.4×10⁻⁴; B = 1, η = 0.01: 2.7×10⁻⁴ vs 4.0×10⁻⁴; B = 1, η = 0.1: 9.6×10⁻³ vs 4.4×10⁻³ (the additive-noise model ignores noise that grows with distance from the optimum); with η_t = 0.1/(1 + t/200) the final excess is 3×10⁻⁶.

sections.title: Where losses come from: maximum likelihood
sections.purpose: Show, starting from a short probability refresher, that a loss is a negative log-likelihood under a noise model, so that choosing a loss becomes choosing an assumption about the noise.
must_cover: Probability refresher, where it is first needed (about 350 words, not an appendix): random variable; probability mass versus density (a density can exceed 1; only its integral is 1); Gaussian N(y; μ, σ²) = (2πσ²)^(−1/2) exp(−(y − μ)²/(2σ²)); Laplace (2b)⁻¹ exp(−|y − μ|/b) with variance 2b²; Bernoulli p^y(1 − p)^(1−y); categorical Π_k p_k^[y=k]; expectation and variance with E[aX + b] = aE[X] + b and Var(aX + b) = a²Var(X) (used in Sections 8 and 12).

Independence and the i.i.d. assumption: the joint probability of independent examples is a product. Say what breaks it in engineering data — repeated measurements of one part, consecutive readings of one sensor — and point to group and time leakage in Section 10.

Likelihood L(θ) = p(D; θ) is a function of θ for fixed data, not a distribution over θ. Take logs because the logarithm is monotone (same maximiser) and because products underflow: 1,000 probabilities of 0.1 multiply to 10⁻¹⁰⁰⁰, which is 0.0 in double precision (smallest normal number about 10⁻³⁰⁸), while the log-likelihood −2302.6 is harmless.

Gaussian noise gives squared error, derived in full: y = f_θ(x) + ε, ε ~ N(0, σ²); log p(D; θ) = −N ln(√(2π)σ) − (1/(2σ²))Σ_i (y_i − f_θ(x_i))². σ does not move the maximiser over θ. Differentiating with respect to σ² gives the MLE σ̂² = (1/N)Σ r_i², which is biased: for a linear model with p parameters E[RSS] = (N − p)σ², so the unbiased estimate divides by N − p (state; cite Bishop or ESL for the proof).

Laplace noise gives absolute error, and the best constant under absolute error is the median (the derivative of |r| is sign(r): equal numbers of residuals above and below); hence robustness to outliers. Huber's loss, quadratic near zero and linear beyond, is the usual compromise (Module 02).
Different noise per point (heteroscedastic Gaussian, σ_i known) gives weighted least squares with weights w_i = 1/σ_i², derived in two lines. This is the likelihood of Section 12's material fit.

The general recipe as a table: noise model → loss → best constant prediction. Gaussian → squared error → mean; Laplace → absolute error → median; Bernoulli → binary cross-entropy → class frequency; categorical → cross-entropy → class frequencies. Choosing a loss is choosing what you believe about the noise.

Cross-entropy and KL in one paragraph: the average negative log-likelihood is the cross-entropy H(p_data, p_θ) = H(p_data) + KL(p_data ‖ p_θ), so maximum likelihood moves the model distribution toward the data distribution. Module 07's perplexity is exp of the per-token cross-entropy.
One-sentence preview: adding a prior over θ turns maximum likelihood into MAP estimation and produces the regularisers of Section 9.
worked_examples: Three residuals r = (0.1, −0.2, 0.3) under σ = 0.2: log-likelihood = −3 ln(√(2π)·0.2) − (0.01 + 0.04 + 0.09)/(2·0.04) = 2.0715 − 1.75 = 0.3215, positive because the densities exceed 1 (the peak density is 1.995). The MLE σ̂² = 0.14/3 = 0.0467 (σ̂ = 0.216) raises it to 0.3403.
A sensor glitch: y = (1.0, 1.2, 0.9, 1.1, 5.0). The squared-error constant is the mean, 1.84, dragged by one point; the absolute-error constant is the median, 1.1.

Cost of an outlier at r = 5 with unit variance: Gaussian negative log-likelihood r²/(2σ²) = 12.5; Laplace with b = 1/√2 (same variance) |r|/b = 7.07. The quadratic penalty is why one bad point can move a least-squares fit.

figures.description: Top panel: Gaussian (σ = 1) and Laplace (b = 1/√2, same variance) densities overlaid on r ∈ [−5, 5]; the Laplace is more peaked with heavier tails. Bottom panel: their negative logs, a parabola and a V, with the outlier at r = 5 marked at 12.5 and 7.07.

checks: A density value of 2.0 comes out of your code. Is something wrong? -> No; densities are not probabilities and exceed 1 when the spread is small; only the integral must equal 1.
Why does the maximum-likelihood θ under Gaussian noise not depend on σ? -> σ multiplies the sum of squares by a positive constant and adds a θ-independent term, so the minimiser does not move.

Which loss would you choose if a few readings in every test are glitches of unknown size? -> An absolute-error or Huber loss (heavy-tailed noise model), or explicit outlier handling; squared error lets one glitch move the fit.

sections.title: Logistic and softmax regression
sections.purpose: Build the linear classifier from the Bernoulli and categorical likelihoods, derive its gradients and convexity, and read its decision boundary — including how it fails on separable data.
must_cover: Model p(y = 1 | x) = σ(wᵀx) with σ(z) = 1/(1 + e^(−z)); properties σ(−z) = 1 − σ(z) and σ′(z) = σ(z)(1 − σ(z)); the logit z = ln(p/(1 − p)) is the log-odds, so logistic regression is linear in the log-odds and a unit change in feature j multiplies the odds by e^(w_j).

Binary cross-entropy as the Bernoulli negative log-likelihood, ℓ = −[y ln p̂ + (1 − y) ln(1 − p̂)]; derive dℓ/dz = p̂ − y with the chain rule written out; data gradient ∇L = (1/N)Xᵀ(p̂ − y), the same shape as least squares with p̂ in place of ŷ.

Hessian (1/N)XᵀSX with S = diag(p̂_i(1 − p̂_i)), positive semidefinite, so the loss is convex; there is no closed form, so use gradient descent or Newton's method (iteratively reweighted least squares); scikit-learn's default solver is L-BFGS. Since S ≤ ¼, λ_max(H) ≤ λ_max(XᵀX/N)/4, which gives the sufficient step bound η < 8/λ_max(XᵀX/N). It is not necessary, because the curvature is far below its worst case wherever p̂ is far from ½: Lab 2 computes the bound 0.59, and in its extension the loss still falls at η = 5.

Why not squared error: with ½(p̂ − y)² the gradient with respect to z is (p̂ − y)p̂(1 − p̂), which vanishes exactly when the model is confidently wrong; squared error through a sigmoid is also non-convex. A confidently wrong model must be able to learn fast.
Stable computation: ℓ = softplus(z) − yz with softplus(z) = max(z, 0) + ln(1 + e^(−|z|)) (np.logaddexp(0, z)); never take ln σ(z) naively. Module 02 generalises this as log-sum-exp.

Decision boundary: predict 1 when p̂ ≥ t; at t = 0.5 that is wᵀx + b ≥ 0, a hyperplane with normal w; the signed distance of x from it is (wᵀx + b)/‖w‖, and ‖w‖ sets how fast the probability changes with distance. A threshold t shifts the boundary in parallel to wᵀx + b = ln(t/(1 − t)). Curved boundaries come from features (x₁², x₂², x₁x₂ give ellipses; Module 02's circle data needs them or a network).

Separable data: if a hyperplane separates the classes, scaling w up lowers every example's loss, the infimum is approached only as ‖w‖ → ∞ and the MLE does not exist; probabilities saturate at 0 and 1. Regularisation (Section 9) or early stopping is required — scikit-learn's default C = 1.0 is an L2 penalty, and Lab 2 shows the weights growing without it.

Softmax regression: logits z = Wx; p̂_k = e^(z_k)/Σ_j e^(z_j); loss −ln p̂_y = −z_y + ln Σ_j e^(z_j); derive ∂ℓ/∂z_k = p̂_k − [k = y] in two cases; matrix form ∇_W L = (1/N)(P̂ − Y)ᵀX. Adding a constant to all logits changes nothing, so one class's weights can be fixed at zero, and with K = 2 softmax reduces to σ(z₁ − z₀) (show). Decision regions meet where two logits tie, (w_j − w_k)ᵀx + (b_j − b_k) = 0: piecewise-linear boundaries.

The same output layer serves every classifier in the series: a language model is a K-way softmax classifier over its vocabulary (tens to hundreds of thousands of entries) at every position (Module 07).
worked_examples: One example, one step: w = (2, −1), b = 0.5, x = (1, 1), y = 0. z = 1.5, p̂ = σ(1.5) = 0.8176, loss −ln(0.1824) = 1.7014. Gradient with respect to z is 0.8176, so ∇w = (0.8176, 0.8176) and ∇b = 0.8176. One step with η = 0.5 gives w = (1.5912, −1.4088), b = 0.0912, new z = 0.2736, p̂ = 0.5680, loss 0.8393. The point's distance from the boundary was 1.5/√5 = 0.671.
Threshold shift: requiring p̂ ≥ 0.9 means z ≥ ln 9 = 2.197, a parallel boundary further into the positive side.
Stable loss at extreme logits: for z = 40, y = 1 the loss is 0.0 to machine precision; for z = −40, y = 1 it is 40.0 — computed without overflow by logaddexp.

Right: per-example losses against z for y = 0 — binary cross-entropy softplus(z), asymptotically linear with slope 1, and ½σ(z)², which saturates at 0.5 with slope tending to zero; the region z > 4 shaded and labelled 'confidently wrong'.

Right: softmax regression on three blobs, three coloured regions with piecewise-linear boundaries meeting at one point.

checks: Show that softmax with two classes is the sigmoid of z₁ − z₀. -> p₁ = e^(z₁)/(e^(z₀) + e^(z₁)) = 1/(1 + e^(−(z₁ − z₀))).

On linearly separable data the weights of unregularised logistic regression keep growing. Why? -> Every positive scaling of a separating w lowers every example's loss, so the loss is minimised only in the limit ‖w‖ → ∞; the MLE does not exist.

sections.title: Measuring a model: metrics, thresholds and calibration
sections.purpose: Choose the metric the decision depends on, read the confusion matrix, ROC and precision–recall curves and calibration, and set a threshold from costs rather than by default.
must_cover: The metric should be the quantity the decision depends on, not the loss (source). Every reported number carries its baseline: an RMSE of 0.3 mm means nothing until you know that predicting the mean gives 1.1 mm and the closed-form solver gives 0.05 mm (source example, kept).

Regression metrics with formulas: RMSE (units of y), MAE (robust to outliers), R² = 1 − SS_res/SS_tot (from Section 2's Pythagoras; the fraction of variance explained relative to predicting the mean; negative on held-out data for a model worse than the mean). Avoid percentage errors when y can be near zero.

The confusion matrix and the rates read from it: accuracy, precision TP/(TP + FP), recall (sensitivity, TPR) TP/(TP + FN), specificity TN/(TN + FP), FPR = 1 − specificity, F1 the harmonic mean of precision and recall (why harmonic: it is low when either is low). State the confusion matrix whenever you state a rate.
Accuracy under imbalance: 99% accuracy at a 1% positive rate is the trivial classifier (source).
The base rate, derived from Bayes' rule: precision = TPR·π/(TPR·π + FPR·(1 − π)) for prevalence π. A good detector on a rare event floods its users with false alarms.

ROC curve (TPR against FPR as the threshold sweeps) and AUC; AUC is the probability that a randomly chosen positive is scored above a randomly chosen negative (Mann–Whitney), so it can be computed by counting pairs. AUC is insensitive to prevalence: good for ranking quality, misleading when positives are rare. The precision–recall curve and average precision (baseline = prevalence) show what the user will experience when positives are rare.

Choosing the threshold for a decision: with calibrated probabilities and costs C_FP and C_FN, predicting positive is cheaper when p·C_FN > (1 − p)·C_FP, i.e. above t* = C_FP/(C_FP + C_FN) (derive in two lines). Or impose a constraint, for example recall ≥ 0.99 at the lowest false-positive rate. Source: cross-entropy minimised, but the decision needed recall at a fixed false-positive rate.

Calibration, defined here for the whole series: a model is calibrated when P(y = 1 | p̂ = p) = p. Reliability diagram; expected calibration error over equal-width bins of p̂, ECE = Σ_b (n_b/N)|freq_b − conf_b|, with conf_b the mean predicted probability and freq_b the fraction of positives in bin b. For K classes, or for a model's answers, the usual form bins the confidence of the predicted class (its largest probability) and compares it with the accuracy in the bin, ECE = Σ_b (n_b/N)|acc_b − conf_b| (the top-label form of Guo et al. 2017; Modules 02, 07 and 09 use it and link here). State the binning (10 or 15 bins is usual, 5 for a test set of about a hundred): ECE changes with it, and it is biased upward on small samples because even a calibrated model's bin frequencies scatter. ECE measures calibration, not discrimination: predicting the base rate for every case is calibrated and useless, so report ECE with the Brier score (1/N)Σ(p̂ − y)², a proper scoring rule, and with the AUC. Models trained long with cross-entropy are usually overconfident (source); recalibrate on held-out data with Platt scaling or isotonic regression (temperature scaling for networks: Module 02 and Module 07).
worked_examples: Weld inspection: 1,000 welds, 50 defective; the model flags 60, of which 40 are defective. TP = 40, FP = 20, FN = 10, TN = 930. Accuracy 0.970, precision 0.667, recall 0.800, F1 0.727, specificity 0.979, FPR 0.021. The trivial 'never defective' rule scores accuracy 0.950 with recall 0.
Base rate: TPR 0.95, FPR 0.05, prevalence 1% gives precision 0.0095/(0.0095 + 0.0495) = 0.161 — five of six alarms are false. At prevalence 0.1% with TPR 0.9 and FPR 0.01, precision is 0.083.
AUC by counting: positives scored 0.8 and 0.6, negatives 0.7 and 0.2; of the four positive–negative pairs, three are ordered correctly (0.6 < 0.7 is the miss), so AUC = 0.75.
Cost-based threshold: if a missed defect costs twenty false alarms (C_FN = 20·C_FP), t* = 1/21 = 0.048.
ECE with three bins: 50 predictions with mean confidence 0.20 and observed frequency 0.10; 30 with 0.50 and 0.50; 20 with 0.90 and 0.70. ECE = (50·0.10 + 30·0 + 20·0.20)/100 = 0.09.

Lab 2's breast-cancer test set (143 cases, 53 malignant): at threshold 0.5, TN 90, FP 0, FN 2, TP 51; accuracy 0.986 against a majority baseline of 0.629; AUC 0.996, average precision 0.994; recall 1.0 needs threshold 0.116 and costs precision (0.828).

Calibrated and useless (Lab 2's test set): predicting the training prevalence 159/426 = 0.373 for every one of the 143 cases puts them all in one bin whose frequency is 53/143 = 0.371, so ECE = 0.003, lower than the fitted model's 0.023, while the AUC is 0.500 and the Brier score 0.233 against the model's 0.023.

figures.description: The weld confusion matrix as a 2×2 grid (rows: actual defective / good; columns: flagged / not flagged) with counts TP 40, FN 10, FP 20, TN 930; brackets show precision reading down the 'flagged' column and recall reading across the 'defective' row.

Side by side for Lab 2's logistic regression on the test set: the ROC curve with the chance diagonal and AUC 0.996 in the legend, and the precision–recall curve with a horizontal baseline at the prevalence 0.371; the operating point for threshold 0.5 marked on both, plus the point for threshold 0.116 (recall 1.0).

Reliability diagram: mean predicted probability per bin (x) against observed frequency (y), with the diagonal for perfect calibration; bars for an overconfident model fall below the diagonal at high confidence; an inset histogram shows how many predictions fall in each bin; ECE printed in the title. Use Lab 2's predictions with 5 bins and note the small test set.

checks: A model has AUC 0.95 and positives are 0.1% of the data. Will its precision be high at 90% recall? -> Not necessarily: at a false-positive rate of even 1%, false alarms outnumber true ones about eleven to one; look at the precision–recall curve.

Why is F1 a harmonic rather than an arithmetic mean? -> The harmonic mean is dominated by the smaller value, so a classifier cannot score well by maximising one of precision or recall at the expense of the other.

sections.title: Generalisation: capacity, bias–variance and cross-validation
sections.purpose: Make overfitting measurable: the three-way split, the capacity curve, the bias–variance decomposition derived, learning curves, k-fold cross-validation and an honest account of double descent.
must_cover: Split before doing anything else (source): training set (what the optimiser sees), validation set (to choose between models and settings), test set (touched once at the end; every look that changes something turns it into a validation set). The test-set discipline is developed in Section 10.

The capacity experiment, set up exactly as in Lab 3: y = sin(2πx) + ε, ε ~ N(0, 0.3²), N = 20 training points on an evenly spaced grid x_i = i/19, polynomials of degree 0 to 15 fitted by least squares in a Legendre basis. Training RMSE never increases with degree; validation RMSE falls and then rises: underfitting on the left, overfitting on the right. Capacity knobs elsewhere: number of parameters, tree depth, 1/k in k-NN, 1/λ in ridge.

The bias–variance decomposition derived step by step at a fixed input x: y = f*(x) + ε with E[ε] = 0, Var ε = σ², ε independent of the training set D; write f̂ = f̂_D(x) and f̄ = E_D[f̂]; expand (f̂ − y)² = ((f̂ − f̄) + (f̄ − f*) − ε)²; the cross terms vanish because E_D[f̂ − f̄] = 0 and ε has mean zero and is independent of D; result E[(f̂ − y)²] = (f̄ − f*)² + E[(f̂ − f̄)²] + σ². Average over x for the expected test error.

Reading it: bias is what the family cannot represent, variance is how much the fit changes with the sample, noise is irreducible. Simple models have high bias and low variance, flexible ones the reverse. The decomposition is exact for squared error; for 0–1 loss there is no clean additive version, only a useful picture.

Learning curves: training and validation error against N for a fixed model. Both approach bias² + σ² from opposite sides. A large persistent gap means variance (more data helps); both high and close together means bias (more data does not help; more capacity or better features do). The best degree moves right as N grows (source exercise 2).

k-fold cross-validation (source): split into k folds, train on k − 1, validate on the remaining one, rotate, average. Choices: k = 5 or 10; stratify classes; leave-one-out for tiny data. The mean comes with a standard error sd/√k, which is approximate and optimistic because folds share training data; it is still the only honest way to say that one setting beats another by less than the noise.

Double descent, honestly: when models are fitted to interpolation and the fitting rule picks the minimum-norm solution, test error can peak where the number of parameters reaches the number of training points (the interpolation threshold) and fall again beyond it (Belkin et al. 2019; Nakkiran et al. 2020 for deep networks). It does not contradict the decomposition, which is an identity; it changes how variance behaves with size when the fitting procedure prefers small-norm solutions. Practical consequence: do not assume a single U; measure on validation data. The guided reading of this session is the Belkin paper.
worked_examples: One training set (Lab 3, seed 0), train/validation RMSE: degree 0 0.850/0.769; 1 0.655/0.536; 3 0.217/0.354; 4 0.217/0.354; 5 0.183/0.360; 9 0.173/0.365; 12 0.141/0.393; 15 0.112/0.720. Best validation degree 3 or 4 (they tie: sin(2πx) is odd about x = ½, so adding an even-degree term buys almost nothing — bias² falls in pairs).

Exact decomposition for this fixed design (smoother-matrix formulas; a 200-draw Monte Carlo in Lab 3 agrees): degree 0: bias² 0.4975, variance 0.0045, total 0.5920; degree 1: 0.2051, 0.0086, 0.3037; degree 3: 0.0052, 0.0161, 0.1113 (the minimum); degree 5: 0.0000, 0.0236, 0.1136; degree 9: 0.0000, 0.0422, 0.1322; degree 12: 0.0000, 0.0754, 0.1654; degree 15: 0.0000, 0.8737, 0.9637 (total includes σ² = 0.09).

Ten times more data (N = 200): degree 3 total 0.0964 (bias² 0.0046, variance 0.0018), degree 5 0.0927 (the new minimum), degree 15 0.0972. Variance fell tenfold, so flexible models stop being punished and the curve flattens.

A biased estimator can win (preview of Section 9 and exercise e7): estimate a mean μ = 1 from n = 4 readings with σ = 2. The sample mean has bias 0 and variance σ²/n = 1, MSE 1.0; half the sample mean has bias² 0.25 and variance 0.25, MSE 0.5.

figures.description: Left: three panels of polynomial fits of degree 1, 3 and 15 to the same 20 noisy samples of sin(2πx), true function dashed, showing underfit, good fit and a wiggly overfit that passes near every point and swings at the ends. Right: training and validation RMSE against degree 0–15 (log y), training monotonically decreasing, validation U-shaped with its minimum at degree 3–4; horizontal dashed line at σ = 0.3; underfitting and overfitting regions shaded.

Bias², variance, noise σ² and their sum against degree 0–15 (log y) for N = 20 and σ = 0.3, from the exact formulas: bias² falling in steps (pairs of degrees), variance rising slowly then sharply after degree 12, the sum U-shaped with its minimum marked at degree 3.

Learning curves: expected training and validation MSE against N from 10 to 1000 (log x) for degree 3 and degree 9; both pairs converge toward σ² + bias²; degree 9 has the larger gap at small N and the lower asymptote.

Schematic double-descent curve: test error against the number of parameters p, the classical U on the left, a peak at the interpolation threshold p = N, and a second descent to the right; regions labelled 'classical regime' and 'interpolating regime'; a note that the right side assumes a minimum-norm fit.

Five-fold cross-validation as a grid: five rows (rounds), each a bar of five blocks with a different block shaded as validation; a separate test block at the right drawn outside the loop with a padlock symbol.

checks: A degree-15 polynomial fitted to 16 points has zero training error. What will its validation error be like, and why? -> Large: it interpolates the noise, and variance dominates.
Your learning curves sit together at a validation MSE of 0.20 with σ² = 0.05 and stay flat as N grows. What do you do? -> High bias: more data will not help; add capacity or better features.
Why is the cross-validation standard error sd/√k optimistic? -> The k fold estimates are positively correlated because their training sets overlap, so their mean varies more than sd/√k suggests.

sections.title: Regularisation as prior knowledge: ridge, lasso and MAP
sections.purpose: Trade variance for bias on purpose, and show that ridge and lasso are maximum a posteriori estimates under Gaussian and Laplace priors, with their shrinkage written out.
must_cover: Bayes' rule p(θ | D) ∝ p(D | θ)p(θ); MAP maximises log p(D | θ) + log p(θ); the prior is the regulariser.

Ridge as MAP, constants kept: Gaussian noise σ² and prior w ~ N(0, τ²I) give the negative log-posterior (1/(2σ²))‖Xw − y‖² + (1/(2τ²))‖w‖² + const; multiplying by 2σ²/N gives (1/N)‖Xw − y‖² + λ‖w‖² with λ = σ²/(Nτ²). More data shrinks the effective penalty; a tighter prior enlarges it.
Ridge closed form: (2/N)Xᵀ(Xw − y) + 2λw = 0 gives (XᵀX + λNI)w = Xᵀy (source). The eigenvalues of XᵀX + λNI are μ_i + λN ≥ λN > 0, so the system is always solvable, even with more columns than rows.

SVD view: with X = UΣVᵀ and singular values s_i, the ridge fit is ŷ = Σ_i u_i [s_i²/(s_i² + λN)] u_iᵀy. Each direction is shrunk by its own factor; directions the data barely constrain (small s_i) are pulled to zero instead of being set by noise (source). Effective degrees of freedom df(λ) = Σ_i s_i²/(s_i² + λN) fall from d + 1 to 0. Use s_i² rather than λ_i here to avoid a clash with the regularisation λ.
Weight decay: the gradient step on the ridge loss is w ← (1 − 2ηλ)w − η∇L, which is why the penalty is called weight decay (source); AdamW's decoupled version is in Module 02.

Lasso as MAP under a Laplace prior p(w_j) ∝ exp(−|w_j|/b): penalty λ‖w‖₁; it drives coefficients exactly to zero and so selects features (source). Geometry: the L1 ball has corners on the axes, which the elliptical loss contours tend to touch first. Orthonormal design (XᵀX = NI) solved exactly: with ŵ the least-squares solution, ridge gives w_j = ŵ_j/(1 + λ) and lasso gives soft-thresholding w_j = sign(ŵ_j)·max(|ŵ_j| − λ/2, 0) (derive per coordinate). Ridge scales; lasso subtracts and clips. In general the lasso has no closed form (coordinate descent); the elastic net mixes L1 and L2 for correlated features.

Practice: standardise before penalising (the penalty is not scale-invariant: a coefficient's size depends on its feature's units); do not penalise the intercept (centre y or exclude b); choose λ on a log grid by validation or cross-validation (source); the one-standard-error rule picks the largest λ whose CV error is within one standard error of the best (Hastie et al.).

Library conventions, so readers can map this λ to code: scikit-learn Ridge minimises ‖y − Xw‖² + α‖w‖², so α = λN; Lasso minimises (1/(2N))‖y − Xw‖² + α‖w‖₁, so α = λ/2; LogisticRegression minimises ½‖w‖² + C·Σ loss_i, so C = 1/(2Nλ).

Other regularisers (source): early stopping (gradient descent from zero applies filter factors 1 − (1 − ηh_i)^t to the eigendirections, behaving roughly like ridge with λ shrinking as ηt grows); data augmentation; dropout and noise injection (Module 02).
worked_examples: Shrinkage factors: XᵀX with eigenvalues 100 and 0.01, λN = 1. Factors 100/101 = 0.990 and 0.01/1.01 = 0.0099: the well-determined direction is untouched, the poorly determined one nearly removed. The condition number of the system falls from 10⁴ to 101/1.01 = 100.
Ridge against lasso, orthonormal design, ŵ = (3.0, 0.4, −1.2), λ = 1: ridge (1.5, 0.2, −0.6); lasso (2.5, 0.0, −0.7). The small coefficient is removed, the large ones are shifted by 0.5.

Lab 3's ridge path at degree 15 (Legendre basis, constant term unpenalised): λ → 0 gives train/validation RMSE 0.112/0.720; λ = 0.032 gives 0.182/0.335; λ = 10 gives 0.832/0.751. Five-fold CV on the 20 training points picks λ = 0.032, whose test RMSE 0.324 beats the best unregularised degree (degree 3, 0.348) and unregularised degree 15 (0.684). Read as a prior, λ = 0.032 corresponds to τ = σ/√(Nλ) ≈ 0.38 on each Legendre coefficient.

figures.description: Two panels in the (w₁, w₂) plane with elliptical least-squares contours centred at the unconstrained solution: left, a disc (L2 ball) touched by a contour at a point with both coordinates non-zero; right, a diamond (L1 ball) touched at its corner on the w₁ axis, so w₂ = 0.

Coefficient paths on the standardised load_diabetes data (10 features): ridge coefficients shrinking smoothly toward zero as log₁₀λ increases; lasso coefficients reaching zero one at a time; a vertical line at the CV-chosen λ in each panel. x-axis log₁₀λ in this module's convention; caption gives the scikit-learn α mapping.

checks: Doubling N with the prior and noise fixed: what happens to the MAP λ? -> It halves (λ = σ²/(Nτ²)); the data outweigh the prior.

Why standardise features before ridge or lasso? -> The penalty treats all coefficients alike, but a coefficient's size depends on its feature's units, so without scaling the penalty is arbitrary across features.

Lasso sets a coefficient exactly to zero; ridge never does. Why, in one sentence? -> The L1 penalty's derivative does not vanish at zero, so small coefficients are clipped; the L2 penalty's derivative 2λw does, so they are only scaled.

sections.title: Evaluating honestly: leakage, selection and intervals
sections.purpose: Estimate how a model will do on new data without fooling yourself: the forms leakage takes, the optimism of selection and its remedy, distribution shift, an uncertainty on every reported number, and paired methods when two models are compared. This section is the series' reference for standard errors, the bootstrap and McNemar's test.
must_cover: How noisy a test number is: the standard error of an accuracy (any proportion) is √(p(1 − p)/n), and the 95% interval is about ±1.96 standard errors, a normal approximation that fails when fewer than about ten errors or ten successes are observed (use the bootstrap or an exact binomial interval there). Size the test set for the interval you need, not by a fixed percentage: a half-width h needs n ≈ 1.96²p(1 − p)/h².
Test-set reuse (source): looking at the test number and changing the model, repeatedly. The remedy is procedural: open the test set once and report the number with the date.

Selection bias: choosing the best of many configurations on a validation set makes the winner's score optimistic, because the maximum of noisy estimates is biased upward. Nested cross-validation: an inner loop selects, an outer loop scores the whole selection procedure; cost k_outer × k_inner × configurations fits.

Leakage, with an example and a fix for each: (1) preprocessing fitted on all data — scaling, imputation, feature selection, target encoding; fit them inside each fold with a Pipeline (the selection case is the dramatic one; scaling is usually mild); (2) duplicates and near-duplicates across the split; (3) groups — repeated measurements of one part, specimen, patient or machine split by row; split by group (GroupKFold); (4) time — a shuffled time series lets the model train on the future; use forward-chaining splits with a gap (TimeSeriesSplit); (5) target leakage — a feature recorded after the label was known; (6) test-set reuse. The rule (source): split by the unit that will be new at deployment — a new part, a new patient, a new day — never by row.

Distribution shift (source): the test set is drawn from the same P as training and deployment is not. Name covariate shift (inputs change), label shift (class proportions change) and concept drift (the input–output relation changes). Evaluate on data from the conditions the model will meet, even if there is less of it; monitor inputs and outputs in production.

Bootstrap confidence intervals: resample the test set with replacement R = 2,000 times, recompute the metric, take the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles. Paired bootstrap for comparing two models on the same test set: resample indices once per replicate for both models and take the interval of the difference — far narrower than the overlap of two separate intervals suggests, because the models' errors are correlated. Resample groups, not rows, when the data are grouped (cluster bootstrap). Two caveats: the bootstrap over the test set measures test-sampling noise, not the variability from retraining; and when a difference rests on a handful of cases where the models disagree, the percentile interval is too narrow, because no replicate can contain a disagreement that never occurred. Use McNemar's exact test then.

McNemar's test, for two classifiers scored on the same n test cases (McNemar 1947; recommended for comparing classifiers by Dietterich 1998): cases both models get right, or both get wrong, say nothing about which is better; only the discordant ones do: n₁₀ cases that A alone gets right and n₀₁ that B alone gets right. If the models are equally good, each discordant case is a fair coin, so n₁₀ ~ Binomial(n₁₀ + n₀₁, ½), and the exact two-sided p-value is min(1, 2·P(X ≤ min(n₁₀, n₀₁))) (scipy.stats.binomtest). The textbook statistic (n₁₀ − n₀₁)²/(n₁₀ + n₀₁), compared with 3.84 for 5% (χ² with one degree of freedom), is a large-count approximation that rejects too easily at moderate counts; its continuity-corrected form (|n₁₀ − n₀₁| − 1)²/(n₁₀ + n₀₁) tracks the exact test. The exact test costs nothing to compute, so use it, and report the two discordant counts with it.

Modules 07 and 09 apply this section's standard errors, paired bootstrap and McNemar's test to language-model benchmarks and link back here. For evaluating LLM-based applications, which raises its own issues, link to the evaluation module of the AI Agents series rather than repeating it.
worked_examples: Standard error: n = 200, p = 0.90 gives SE = 0.021 and a 95% interval of about ±0.042; n = 2,000 gives ±0.013. A ±0.02 interval at p = 0.90 needs n = 1.96² × 0.09/0.02² ≈ 865 test cases.

The best of 200 equals: 200 configurations whose true accuracy is 0.80, each estimated with SE 0.01. The expected maximum of 200 independent standard normals is 2.746 (computed by integration), so the winner shows about 0.827 although none is better than 0.80. Lab 4's extension makes it concrete: on pure-noise data, the best of 200 random 5-feature subsets scores 0.67 by 5-fold CV; nested CV of the same search gives 0.56.

Lab 4's three leaks in numbers: selection on all 100 rows of pure noise with 5,000 features gives CV accuracy 0.87 ± 0.05 against 0.50 ± 0.10 honestly; 40 specimens × 10 measurements give row-split accuracy 0.95 (random forest) and 1.00 (5-NN) against 0.63 and 0.64 split by specimen; a drifting pump series gives shuffled RMSE 2.33 (noise floor 2.0) against 4.09 with forward chaining. Standardisation fitted on all of load_breast_cancer changes the CV accuracy by less than 0.001.

Paired versus separate intervals, and McNemar (Lab 4): logistic regression and 15-NN on Lab 2's test set score 0.986 and 0.951; separate 95% intervals [0.965, 1.000] and [0.909, 0.986] overlap, yet the paired difference 0.035 has interval [0.007, 0.070], which excludes zero. Only five cases are discordant, all favouring logistic regression (n₁₀ = 5, n₀₁ = 0), and McNemar's exact test gives p = 2 × 0.5⁵ = 0.0625: suggestive, not significant at 5%. The methods disagree because the evidence is five cases: a replicate shows a difference of zero only by drawing none of the five, with probability (138/143)¹⁴³ = 0.006, and no replicate can show 15-NN ahead. Report the difference, the discordant counts and the exact p-value; a larger test set would settle it.

The χ² shortcut at moderate counts: n₁₀ = 24 and n₀₁ = 12 give (24 − 12)²/36 = 4.0 > 3.84, p = 0.046, 'significant'; the exact test gives p = 0.065, and the continuity-corrected statistic 11²/36 = 3.36 gives p = 0.067.

figures.description: Nested cross-validation: an outer ring of five folds; inside each outer training portion a smaller inner three-fold loop choosing λ; arrows show that the outer validation fold only scores the model chosen by the inner loop.

Four splitting schemes for data with groups and time, drawn as coloured timelines of rows (train blue, validation orange): random row split (leaky); group split keeping each specimen's rows together; forward-chaining time split with a gap before each validation block; and a split that respects both.

Bootstrap distributions from Lab 4: histograms of 2,000 replicate accuracies for the two models (overlapping), and the histogram of the paired difference with its 2.5% and 97.5% percentiles marked, clear of zero, and no bar below zero; an annotation gives the discordant counts 5 and 0 and McNemar's exact p = 0.0625.

checks: You standardise with the mean and variance of the whole dataset before cross-validation. Is it leakage, and does it matter? -> Yes, in principle; for scaling the effect is usually negligible (Lab 4 measures under 0.001), but the same habit with feature selection or target encoding can be large. Fit preprocessing inside each fold.
Twenty measurements were taken on each of 30 specimens. How do you split? -> By specimen (GroupKFold), so no specimen contributes rows to both training and validation.

Why compare two models with a paired bootstrap rather than two separate intervals? -> They are scored on the same examples, so their errors are correlated; the paired difference cancels the shared difficulty and has a much narrower interval.

Two classifiers disagree on six test cases, all six in A's favour. Is A better at the 5% level? -> McNemar's exact two-sided p = 2 × 0.5⁶ = 0.031, so yes, narrowly; five such cases would give 0.0625. With five or fewer discordant cases no split can reach 5%.

sections.title: Beyond linear: the methods you will meet
sections.purpose: Give a working acquaintance with the classical nonlinear methods and two unsupervised workhorses, with enough mechanism to know when each is the right baseline.
must_cover: k-nearest neighbours (source): predict by averaging or voting over the k closest training points; k is a capacity knob (k = 1 interpolates; large k has high bias); needs scaling because distances mix units; no training, prediction cost about Nd per query; a strong baseline in low dimensions. The curse of dimensionality: a sub-cube holding a fraction r of uniformly spread data has edge r^(1/d), so neighbourhoods stop being local as d grows.

Decision trees: recursive axis-aligned threshold splits chosen to reduce impurity (variance for regression; Gini 1 − Σ_k p_k² or entropy for classification); depth is capacity; invariant to monotone rescaling of features, so no scaling needed; high variance.

Random forests (source): trees grown on bootstrap samples with a random subset of features considered at each split, then averaged. For M trees of variance σ² and pairwise correlation ρ, the average has variance ρσ² + (1 − ρ)σ²/M (state with a one-line derivation): decorrelating trees matters more than adding them. Out-of-bag error as a free validation estimate.

Gradient boosting (source): an additive model F_m = F_(m−1) + νh_m in which each small tree h_m is fitted to the negative gradient of the loss at F_(m−1) — for squared error, the residuals. Gradient descent in function space, with ν the learning rate traded against the number of trees and early stopping on validation. Implementations: XGBoost, LightGBM, scikit-learn's HistGradientBoosting (as of 2026). On tabular data of up to a few hundred thousand rows it is very often the best method and the first thing to try (source), needs no scaling, handles missing values natively; cite Grinsztajn et al. (2022) for the benchmark evidence, and say that exercise e13 tests the claim, including a dataset where it loses.

Kernels and SVMs, about 400 words with the derivation written out: replace x by a feature map φ(x) and stack the mapped inputs as the rows of Φ. Ridge gives w = (ΦᵀΦ + λNI)⁻¹Φᵀy; the push-through identity (ΦᵀΦ + λNI)⁻¹Φᵀ = Φᵀ(ΦΦᵀ + λNI)⁻¹ (one line: (ΦᵀΦ + λNI)Φᵀ = Φᵀ(ΦΦᵀ + λNI), then multiply by both inverses) turns it into w = Φᵀα with α = (K + λNI)⁻¹y and K = ΦΦᵀ, so f(x) = Σ_i α_i k(x_i, x) needs only inner products k(x, x′) = φ(x)ᵀφ(x′): the kernel trick, and kernel ridge regression. The RBF kernel exp(−γ‖x − x′‖²) corresponds to an infinite-dimensional φ that is never formed. Cost O(N³) to fit and N kernel evaluations per prediction. The SVM uses the hinge loss max(0, 1 − y f(x)) with an L2 penalty: a maximum-margin boundary determined by the support vectors, the training points on or inside the margin, so prediction needs only those. State of the art on medium-sized data before deep learning (source).

Gaussian processes (source): a distribution over functions giving an uncertainty with every prediction; cubic cost in N; surrogate models for expensive engineering simulations and Bayesian optimisation. The GP posterior mean is kernel ridge regression with λN equal to the noise variance.
Neural networks (source): features are learned; their advantage is on images, text and signals where good features are not known and data are plentiful (the rest of the series).

k-means: Lloyd's algorithm alternates assigning points to the nearest centre and moving each centre to its cluster mean; the objective Σ‖x − μ_c‖² never increases, but the result depends on the start (use k-means++ and several restarts); choose k by the downstream use, the elbow or silhouette; needs scaling.

PCA: the directions of maximal variance are the eigenvectors of the sample covariance, equivalently the right singular vectors of the centred data; explained-variance ratio λ_i/Σλ; projection z = V_kᵀ(x − μ). Uses: visualisation, compression, denoising, decorrelating features (which improves conditioning, Section 3). Linear only; sensitive to scaling. Neural forms (autoencoders) are in Module 05.
No free lunch (source): averaged over all possible problems no method beats another (Wolpert 1996), which is why the evaluation of Sections 7–10 matters more than the choice of method.
A comparison table: method | capacity knob | needs scaling? | fit cost | prediction cost | handles interactions? | typical first use.

In gradient boosting with squared error, what is each new tree fitted to? -> The residuals y − F_(m−1)(x), which are the negative gradient of ½(y − F)².

sections.title: Engineering case: fitting a hyperelastic material model
sections.purpose: Apply every ingredient of the module to a realistic engineering fit — a soft hydrogel in uniaxial compression — including weighted and nonlinear least squares, residual analysis, the parameters' uncertainty and the limits of extrapolation.
must_cover: The physics in about 150 words: an incompressible neo-Hookean solid has strain energy W = c₁(I₁ − 3); in uniaxial stretch λ (λ < 1 in compression) the principal stretches are (λ, λ^(−1/2), λ^(−1/2)) and I₁ = λ² + 2/λ; the nominal stress is P = dW/dλ = 2c₁(λ − λ⁻²) = 2c₁g(λ). Shear modulus μ = 2c₁ and small-strain Young's modulus E = 6c₁. Flag the symbol clash: λ is a stretch in this section only.

Weighted least squares and the coefficient's uncertainty: the model is linear in c₁ once g is computed (source). Each point has a recorded uncertainty σ_i, so the likelihood is Gaussian with a different variance per point (Section 5) and maximising it is weighted least squares: minimise Σ_i w_i(P_i − 2c₁g_i)² with w_i = 1/σ_i². Derive c₁* = Σw_iP_ig_i/(2Σw_ig_i²). The estimate is linear in the P_i, so its uncertainty follows by propagation (source): c₁* = Σa_iP_i with a_i = w_ig_i/(2Σw_jg_j²), so Var(c₁*) = Σa_i²σ_i² = 1/(4Σw_ig_i²), a standard deviation that is a function of the measurements', not an opinion; Lab 5 checks it by Monte Carlo.

Goodness of fit: normalised residuals r_i = (P_i − P̂_i)/σ_i and the reduced chi-square χ²_ν = Σr_i²/(N − p), about 1 when the model and the σ_i are right; runs of same-signed residuals indicate a wrong model. Report the RMS residual normalised by the largest measured stress (makes different specimens comparable) and the strain range fitted over.

Extrapolation: a fit over 0–20% says nothing about 40% (source). The parameter interval quantifies noise given the model; it does not include model error. The fitted range travels with the model, and the model is used only where it was evaluated — Section 8 in one sentence.

Nonlinear least squares, with a richer model: the Gent model P = 2c₁g(λ)/(1 − β(I₁ − 3)), β = 1/J_m ≥ 0 (finite chain extensibility), contains neo-Hookean as β = 0 and is nonlinear in β. Gauss–Newton linearises the residuals, θ ← θ − (JᵀWJ)⁻¹JᵀWr; Levenberg–Marquardt and trust-region methods add damping. scipy.optimize.least_squares on weighted residuals returns J at the solution, and Cov(θ̂) ≈ (JᵀWJ)⁻¹ (scale by χ²_ν if the σ_i are only known up to a factor). Parameters fitted together are correlated; a parameter can be undetermined by data that do not exercise it: I₁ − 3 ≈ 3ε² at small strain ε, so β changes the stress by under 1% below 10% strain.

The loading direction, and refusing inputs (source, generalised): g is not symmetric about λ = 1, so the direction must be declared; reading compression data as tension gives a wrong coefficient, and over a small range the residuals do not reveal it — a wrong model can fit well. A fitting routine should therefore refuse inputs it cannot honour — a point without an uncertainty, stresses whose sign contradicts the declared direction, a fitted non-positive stiffness — and say why instead of returning a number; that is what a learning method should do when its assumptions are violated. (The case's five-ingredient table is in Section 1 and in the session review; do not repeat it here.)
worked_examples: Lab 5's synthetic test (true material Gent with c₁ = 10 kPa, β = 0.2; 16 stretches 0.975 to 0.600; σ_i = 0.05 kPa + 2% of the stress). Neo-Hookean on strains up to 20% (8 points): c₁ = 10.09 ± 0.10 kPa, χ²_ν = 0.71, normalised RMS residual 1.1% of the largest stress. Extrapolated with its 95% band: at 30% strain −27.06 ± 0.52 kPa against −28.82 (6.1% low); at 40% strain −43.96 ± 0.85 kPa against −50.57 (13.1% low) — the error is about eight times the band.

The same model on all 16 points: c₁ = 10.55 ± 0.06 kPa, χ²_ν = 4.5, residual signs ++++++++++------ (a run of ten then six). Gent on all 16 by nonlinear least squares: c₁ = 9.95 ± 0.10 kPa, β = 0.208 ± 0.024, correlation −0.78, χ²_ν = 0.40; Monte Carlo SDs 0.099 and 0.025 agree with the linearised ones. Gent on the 20% data only: β = 0.21 ± 0.21 — neo-Hookean (β = 0) cannot be excluded.

Loading direction: g(0.8) = −0.7625 but g(1.25) = 0.61. Reading the 0–20% data as tension (λ = 1 + ε) gives c₁ = 12.97 kPa, 28.5% high, with χ²_ν = 20.7; over the first 5% the misread fit is clean (χ²_ν = 0.38) and already 8.7% high.

Normalised residuals (P_i − P̂_i)/σ_i against stretch for two fits to all 16 points: neo-Hookean (a systematic arch, a run of positives then negatives, several beyond ±2) and Gent (scattered within ±2). Horizontal lines at 0 and ±2.

checks: The 95% interval of c₁ is ±1%, yet at 40% strain the neo-Hookean prediction is 13% off. Is that a contradiction? -> No: the interval quantifies noise given the model; it is silent about the model being wrong outside the fitted range.
Why can β not be determined from data below 10% strain? -> I₁ − 3 ≈ 3ε², so β changes the stress by less than 1% there, which is below the noise; the data carry almost no information about β.
