what_goes_wrong: The loss is minimised but the decisions are poor -> the loss is not the objective: cross-entropy was minimised while the decision needs recall at a fixed false-positive rate -> choose the metric and the operating threshold from the decision's costs or constraints (Section 7) and report performance at that operating point.

Gradient descent stalls; 'the model does not learn' -> features unscaled or uncentred, so κ(XᵀX) is huge (10¹⁰ in Lab 1) -> centre and standardise with training statistics; compute κ before blaming the model.
The loss rises or becomes NaN within a few steps -> learning rate above 2/λ_max -> divide η by 3 to 10, or sweep a log grid on a short run and take the largest η whose loss falls smoothly.
SGD's loss stops improving at a noisy plateau -> the constant-step noise floor, proportional to η/B -> decay the step (Robbins–Monro) or enlarge the batch; do not read the plateau as convergence.

Logistic regression's weights grow without limit and its probabilities are all 0 or 1 -> linearly separable training data with no penalty -> keep an L2 penalty (scikit-learn's default C = 1) or stop early, then check calibration.
Excellent cross-validation scores, poor results in service -> rows of the same part, specimen or machine on both sides of the split -> split by the unit that will be new at deployment (GroupKFold).
A time-series model looks prophetic -> a shuffled split lets it train on the future -> forward-chaining splits with a gap (TimeSeriesSplit); never shuffle across time.

High accuracy on data that should be unpredictable -> feature selection or another preprocessing step was fitted on all the data before cross-validation (0.87 on pure noise in Lab 4) -> put every fitted step in a Pipeline evaluated inside the folds.

The validation score of the chosen configuration does not hold up -> the validation set chose among two hundred configurations and the maximum is optimistic by an amount you cannot see -> nested cross-validation, or a test set opened once, with the date of opening recorded.

Accuracy is high and the model is useless -> class imbalance; the model predicts the majority class -> report the confusion matrix, precision and recall and the precision–recall curve, each against the majority-class baseline.

'Model A beats model B by half a point' -> the difference is inside the test set's sampling noise -> compare on the same cases: the discordant counts, McNemar's exact test and a paired bootstrap interval of the difference; say so when the interval includes zero, and trust the exact test when only a handful of cases disagree.
Predicted probabilities do not match observed frequencies -> long cross-entropy training or a shift since training -> reliability diagram and ECE; recalibrate on held-out data (Platt or isotonic).

A model with an excellent ECE is useless -> calibration is not discrimination: predicting the base rate for every case is calibrated (ECE 0.003 on Lab 2's test set against the model's 0.023) -> report ECE with the Brier score and the AUC, and state the binning.

The model is asked to extrapolate, and the fit looked clean -> nothing constrains f outside the data's support, and the parameter interval excludes model error (13% at 40% strain in Lab 5) -> store the fitted range with the model; refuse or flag predictions outside it; collect data where candidate models disagree.

Performance decays months after deployment -> non-stationarity: the process, the sensors or the population changed -> monitor the distributions of inputs and outputs, not only accuracy; retrain or recalibrate on recent data.

labs.title: Linear regression three ways: closed form, gradient descent and SGD
labs.goal: Fit the same linear model by the normal equations, gradient descent and SGD; watch the divergence boundary land exactly at 2/λ_max; make gradient descent fail with badly scaled features and repair it; measure the SGD noise floor.
labs.data: Synthetic, as in the source: rng = np.random.default_rng(0); X = rng.normal(size=(200, 3)); y = X @ [1.5, -2.0, 0.5] + 0.7 + 0.1*rng.normal(size=200). No download.
steps: Generate the data exactly as above and append a column of ones (Xb, shape (200, 4)).

Closed form with np.linalg.solve(Xb.T@Xb, Xb.T@y) and with np.linalg.lstsq; print both rounded to 3 decimals: [1.491, -2.01, 0.505, 0.696]. Print the residual RMS 0.1000 and sqrt(RSS/(N - 4)) = 0.1010: the noise level, recovered.
Form H = (2/N) Xb.T @ Xb; print its eigenvalues [1.711, 1.922, 2.126, 2.207], κ = 1.29, η_max = 2/λ_max = 0.906 and η* = 2/(λ_max + λ_min) = 0.511.
Gradient descent from zeros: η = 0.1 for 500 steps prints the same 3-decimal vector as the closed form (the source's loop). Count steps until ‖w − w*‖ < 1e-6: 76 at η = 0.1, 7 at η*.

Learning-rate sweep for 200 steps at η = f·η_max, f ∈ {0.5, 0.9, 0.99, 1.01, 1.1, 1.5}; print the final training MSE: 0.0100, 0.0100, 0.0104 (still ringing, ‖w − w*‖ = 0.020), 3.8e3, 6.5e31, 3.5e120. Plot loss against step (log y) for f = 0.5, 0.99, 1.01.

Bad units: copy X, multiply column 0 by 1000 and add 100 to column 1. Print κ = 1.0e10 and η_max = 9.7e-7; print κ with only the scaling (1.1e6) and only the offset (1.0e8). Run 100,000 GD steps at 0.9η_max (under a second): the training MSE is still 4.28 against 0.0100 from lstsq on the same data.

Standardise with the training mean and standard deviation; print κ = 1.22; GD at η* converges in 6 steps; map the weights back to original units (w_j/s_j and b − Σ μ_j w_j/s_j) and print them equal to the lstsq solution of the badly scaled problem.

Mini-batch SGD with per-epoch shuffling (permutations from default_rng(1)), 50 epochs, configurations (B, η) = (200, 0.1), (32, 0.1), (10, 0.1), (1, 0.1), (1, 0.03), (1, 0.01) and (1, η_t = 0.1/(1 + t/200)). Record the excess training loss after every update. Print the mean over the second half of updates next to the prediction Σ_i ηs²λ_i/(B(2 − ηλ_i)) with s² = 0.0100 (per-example gradient noise near the optimum ≈ 2s²H): about 1.0e-4 vs 1.4e-4 (B = 32), 3.1e-4 vs 4.4e-4 (B = 10), 2.7e-4 vs 4.0e-4 (B = 1, η = 0.01), 1.3e-3 vs 1.2e-3 (B = 1, η = 0.03), 9.6e-3 vs 4.4e-3 (B = 1, η = 0.1); the decaying schedule ends near 3e-6.
Plot excess loss against update number (log–log) for full batch, B = 32, B = 1 and B = 1 with decay, with the predicted floors dashed: this is fig-01-6.
expected_observations: Closed form, lstsq and gradient descent agree to three decimals; the residual RMS equals the noise standard deviation, so nothing recoverable is left.
The divergence boundary is sharp and lands where the eigenvalue analysis puts it: 0.99η_max converges, 1.01η_max explodes.

With bad units gradient descent appears not to learn although the model is fine; centring and scaling restore convergence in six steps. The fix is a change of variables, not a new algorithm, and the closed form never noticed the problem.

Constant-step SGD hovers at a floor roughly proportional to η/B; the predictions agree within about a factor of two (the additive-noise model ignores gradient noise that grows away from the optimum, which matters most at B = 1, η = 0.1); a decaying step goes below every floor.
extensions: Add a fifth column equal to 0.99·(column 0) + 0.01·noise, standardise everything and watch κ and the GD step count grow: correlation, not units.
Replace the fixed step by backtracking (halve η until the loss decreases) and compare step counts with η*.
Time np.linalg.lstsq against 100 GD steps for N = 10⁶, d = 100 and decide which you would use.

labs.title: Logistic regression from scratch, and the metrics a decision needs
labs.goal: Implement regularised logistic regression with a numerically stable loss, match scikit-learn, then measure the classifier the way a decision needs: confusion matrix, thresholds for a recall target, ROC and precision–recall curves, calibration — and watch the weights diverge on separable data without a penalty.
labs.data: scikit-learn's built-in load_breast_cancer (569 cases, 30 features; ships with the package, no download). Positive class = malignant, so y = 1 − data.target (scikit-learn codes malignant as 0). Stratified 75/25 split with random_state=0: training 426 (159 malignant), test 143 (53 malignant).
steps: Load, flip the target, print class counts (212 malignant, 357 benign) and split sizes; standardise with training statistics.

Write the loss mean(np.logaddexp(0, z) − y·z) + λ‖w‖² (intercept unpenalised) with λ = 1/(2NC), C = 1, and its gradient (1/N)Aᵀ(p̂ − y) + 2λw. Print the curvature bound λ_max(AᵀA/N)/4 = 3.39, hence η < 0.59; use η = 0.5.
Gradient check at a random w with central differences (ε = 1e-6): print the relative error ‖g_num − g‖/‖g_num + g‖ (about 1e-10). This habit returns in Module 02.
Run 20,000 GD steps (under a second); print the loss at steps 10, 100, 1,000 and 20,000: 0.123, 0.0760, 0.0685, 0.0684.

Fit LogisticRegression(C=1.0, tol=1e-8, max_iter=10_000) on the same standardised data; print the largest coefficient difference (about 1e-6). Then show that the default tol=1e-4 leaves a difference of 0.016: a stopping rule, not a different model.
Test-set probabilities; at threshold 0.5 print the confusion matrix [[TN 90, FP 0], [FN 2, TP 51]], accuracy 0.986, precision 1.000, recall 0.962, F1 0.981, and the majority-class baseline 0.629.
ROC AUC 0.996 and average precision 0.994; plot the ROC and precision–recall curves with the threshold-0.5 point and the PR baseline at prevalence 53/143 = 0.371 (fig-01-11).
Thresholds for recall targets from precision_recall_curve: recall ≥ 0.98 needs threshold 0.219 (precision 0.852); recall = 1.0 needs 0.116 (precision 0.828). Print the table.

Calibration: reliability diagram with 5 equal-width bins, Brier score 0.023, ECE 0.023; note that 143 test cases make the bins noisy (fig-01-12). Then score the constant predictor that outputs the training prevalence 159/426 = 0.373 for every case: ECE 0.003, Brier 0.233, AUC 0.500, better calibrated than the model and useless.

Separable data: rerun gradient descent with λ = 0 and η = 1.0 and print ‖w‖ after 100, 1,000, 10,000 and 100,000 steps: 3.2, 6.2, 16.1, 51.2; the training loss falls toward zero (0.0088) and the training errors reach 0. About one second.
expected_observations: The from-scratch model and scikit-learn agree once both have converged; disagreements of 10⁻² come from a solver tolerance, which is worth knowing before blaming either.
AUC 0.996 says the ranking is excellent; the threshold is still a decision: catching every malignant case costs precision 0.83 instead of 1.00.
Accuracy 0.986 means something only next to the 0.629 baseline.
Without a penalty on separable data ‖w‖ grows roughly like the logarithm of the step count and the probabilities saturate; the default L2 penalty is what prevents it.
ECE alone would rank the constant predictor (0.003) above the model (0.023); the Brier score (0.233 against 0.023) and the AUC do not: calibration is not discrimination.
extensions: Softmax regression on load_iris with your own gradient (P̂ − Y)ᵀX/N; compare with LogisticRegression.
Repeat step 4 with η = 2 and η = 5: the loss still falls. The bound η < 2/L is sufficient, not necessary, for this non-quadratic loss.
Recalibrate with CalibratedClassifierCV(method='sigmoid', cv=5) on the training set and compare Brier scores.

labs.title: Polynomials: capacity, bias–variance and the ridge path
labs.goal: Reproduce the capacity curve, estimate bias² and variance by Monte Carlo and check them against exact formulas, trace the ridge path at degree 15, and choose λ by five-fold cross-validation.
labs.data: Synthetic: f(x) = sin(2πx), σ = 0.3. rng = np.random.default_rng(0); training x = np.linspace(0, 1, 20) (fixed design) with y = f(x) + 0.3·rng.normal(size=20); then validation x = rng.uniform(0, 1, 1000) with its noise; then test x = rng.uniform(0, 1, 10000) with its noise (draw in this order). Features legvander(2x − 1, d) from numpy.polynomial.legendre.
steps: Generate the data; print the condition number of the Legendre design at d = 15 (about 47) next to the monomial Vandermonde in t = 2x − 1 (about 6.7e5): the basis matters numerically.
Plot fits for degrees 1, 3 and 15 and the RMSE-against-degree curve (fig-01-13).

Monte Carlo: 200 fresh noise draws on the same x; for every degree compute the mean prediction and the variance on 201 grid points; print bias², variance and their sum + σ²: for example d3 0.0052/0.016, d9 0.0002/0.042, d15 about 0.005/0.93. Then compute the exact values with the smoother matrix S = Φ_grid R⁻¹Qᵀ (bias² = mean (S f − f_grid)², variance = σ² mean of row sums of S²): d3 0.0052/0.0161, d9 0.0000/0.0422, d15 0.0000/0.8737. Explain the gap: the Monte Carlo bias² includes variance/200.

Ridge at degree 15 with the constant term unpenalised: solve (ΦᵀΦ + λN·I′)w = Φᵀy over λ in np.logspace(−10, 1, 23); print train/validation RMSE and ‖w‖: λ → 0 gives 0.112/0.720; λ = 0.032 gives 0.182/0.335; λ = 10 gives 0.832/0.751.

Five-fold CV on the 20 training points (indices permuted by default_rng(0), np.array_split into 5): CV chooses λ = 0.032 (the one-standard-error rule picks the same here). Test RMSE of the refit model 0.324, against 0.348 for unregularised degree 3 and 0.684 for unregularised degree 15.
Library check: sklearn.linear_model.Ridge(alpha=λ·N) on the features without the constant column, fit_intercept=True, reproduces the coefficients to about 1e-15.
Ten times more data (source exercise 2): repeat step 2 with N = 200 (same draw order); the best validation degree moves to about 5, and degrees 5 to 15 all sit within 0.01 of RMSE 0.30.
expected_observations: Training RMSE never increases with degree; validation RMSE falls to about 0.35 and climbs to 0.72 at degree 15.
bias² + variance + σ² reproduces the validation MSE; bias² falls in pairs (degrees 1 and 2, 3 and 4) because sin(2πx) is odd about x = ½.
A regularised degree-15 model (test 0.324) beats the best small unregularised model (0.348): shrinking a flexible model can beat choosing a small one.
With 200 points the variance term is about ten times smaller and flexible models stop being punished.
extensions: Use raw monomials xᵏ with the normal equations at d = 15 and watch the solution change with rounding (κ(ΦᵀΦ) = κ(Φ)²).
Learning curves: expected train and validation MSE for N from 10 to 1,000 at degrees 3 and 9 (fig-01-15).
Leave-one-out CV (k = 20) against five-fold: compare the chosen λ and the spread of the fold errors.

labs.title: The leakage clinic
labs.goal: Build three pipelines that report excellent scores for the wrong reason, repair each, and put bootstrap confidence intervals on honest results, paired where models are compared, with McNemar's exact test on the cases where two models disagree.
labs.data: Synthetic generators below plus load_breast_cancer (built in). No download.
steps: Leak 1, selection before cross-validation: rng = default_rng(0); X = rng.normal(size=(100, 5000)); y = rng.integers(0, 2, 100) — pure noise. Leaky: SelectKBest(f_classif, k=20) fitted on all 100 rows, then StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0) CV of LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000) on the selected columns: 0.87 ± 0.05. Honest: make_pipeline(SelectKBest, LogisticRegression) under the same CV: 0.50 ± 0.10. Repeat with seeds 1–3: leaky 0.83–0.92, honest 0.45–0.58.
The mild case: StandardScaler fitted on all of load_breast_cancer before 5-fold CV against the scaler inside the pipeline: 0.9789 in both. The leak exists in principle and is negligible for scaling.

Leak 2, groups: rng = default_rng(0); 40 specimens with labels rng.integers(0, 2, 40) and fingerprints rng.normal(0, 1, (40, 10)); each specimen gets 10 rows = fingerprint + 0.3·rng.normal(size=(10, 10)), with column 0 shifted by 0.3·(2y − 1) (a weak real signal). Row-wise KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0): random forest (300 trees) 0.95, 5-NN (scaled) 1.00. GroupKFold(5) by specimen: 0.63 ± 0.14 and 0.64 ± 0.14.

Leak 3, time: a pump's bearing temperature over 120 days, hourly. rng = default_rng(0); t = arange(2880); hour = t % 24; drift = cumsum(rng.normal(0, 0.2, 2880)); temp = 10 + 8 sin(2π(hour − 9)/24) + rng.normal(0, 1, 2880); y = 50 + 0.8·temp + 5 sin(2π·hour/24) + drift + rng.normal(0, 2, 2880). Features (t, hour, temp); RandomForestRegressor(100, min_samples_leaf=2, random_state=0). Shuffled KFold: RMSE 2.33 (R² 0.88). TimeSeriesSplit(5, gap=24): RMSE 4.09 (R² −0.01). The noise floor is 2.0.

Intervals: on Lab 2's split, fit pipelines StandardScaler + LogisticRegression(C=1) and StandardScaler + KNeighborsClassifier(15); test accuracies 0.986 (2 errors) and 0.951 (7 errors). Percentile bootstrap with R = 2,000 replicates and default_rng(0): [0.965, 1.000] and [0.909, 0.986], overlapping. Paired bootstrap of the difference (same resampled indices for both): 0.035 [0.007, 0.070]; the fraction of replicates with difference ≤ 0 is about 0.006, the chance (138/143)¹⁴³ of drawing none of the discordant cases. Discordant cases 5 versus 0; McNemar's exact test, scipy.stats.binomtest(5, 5, 0.5).pvalue = 0.0625. Print the χ² statistic 5.0 (p = 0.025) and its continuity-corrected form 3.2 (p = 0.074) beside it, to show the large-count formula overstating the evidence.
Print a summary table: case | leaky score | honest score | the fix.
expected_observations: Selecting features on all the data manufactures 87% accuracy from noise; inside the pipeline the score returns to chance.

Split by row, the models recognise specimens rather than learning the property; split by specimen they are near chance with a wide spread, which is the honest picture of 40 specimens and a weak signal.
The shuffled time-series score is at the noise floor because the forest interpolates the drift from neighbouring hours; forward chaining shows it cannot forecast the drift.

Separate intervals overlap while the paired interval excludes zero, so comparisons need paired methods. Yet McNemar's exact test (p = 0.0625) does not reject at 5%: with five discordant cases the bootstrap interval is too narrow, and the honest summary is the difference, the counts 5 and 0 and the exact p-value.
extensions: Selection bias: on pure noise (X of shape (100, 50)) score 200 random 5-feature subsets by 5-fold CV: the best reaches about 0.67; wrap the search in an outer 5-fold loop (nested CV) and get about 0.56 (about 30 s).
Cluster bootstrap for Leak 2: resample specimens rather than rows and compare the interval width with the row bootstrap.
Add a 'target leak' column (the label plus small noise) and watch every model become brilliant.

labs.title: Fitting a hyperelastic material model
labs.goal: Fit a neo-Hookean coefficient to a synthetic compression test by weighted least squares, verify its uncertainty, see a clean fit fail by extrapolation, detect the misfit with residuals, fit the Gent model by nonlinear least squares, and refuse inputs the fit cannot honour.
labs.data: Synthetic compression test of a soft hydrogel. Stretches λ = 1 − 0.025·k, k = 1..16 (0.975 to 0.600, strain 2.5% to 40%). True material: Gent with c₁ = 10 kPa, β = 0.2, i.e. P = 2c₁(λ − λ⁻²)/(1 − β(λ² + 2/λ − 3)). Recorded uncertainty σ_i = 0.05 kPa + 0.02|P_true,i|; P = P_true + σ·default_rng(1).normal(size=16).
steps: Define g, I₁ − 3, P_NH and P_Gent; generate the data; print the table of λ, P and σ (P from −1.51 to −49.93 kPa).

check_inputs(λ, P, σ, direction) raises ValueError, with a message, for a missing or non-positive σ, stretches on the wrong side of 1 for the declared direction, and stresses of the wrong sign. Demonstrate three refusals.

Weighted least squares, closed form, on strains up to 20% (first 8 points): c₁ = 10.09 ± 0.10 kPa, χ²_ν = 0.71, normalised residuals within ±1.3, RMS residual 1.1% of the largest stress. Confirm with scipy.optimize.least_squares on the weighted residuals (same c₁).
Monte Carlo check: 1,000 refits to the fitted curve plus fresh noise with the same σ_i (default_rng(2)): SD 0.0995 against the formula's 0.0997.
Extrapolate with a 95% band from Var(c₁): at λ = 0.7, −27.06 ± 0.52 kPa against the true −28.82 (−6.1%); at λ = 0.6, −43.96 ± 0.85 against −50.57 (−13.1%).
Neo-Hookean on all 16 points: c₁ = 10.55 ± 0.06, χ²_ν = 4.5; print the residual signs ++++++++++------.

Gent by nonlinear least squares (least_squares, x0 = (5, 0), bounds c₁ ≥ 0 and 0 ≤ β < 1/max(I₁ − 3), x_scale='jac'); covariance (JᵀJ)⁻¹ from the returned Jacobian of the weighted residuals. All 16 points: c₁ = 9.95 ± 0.10, β = 0.208 ± 0.024, correlation −0.78, χ²_ν = 0.40; Monte Carlo SDs 0.099 and 0.025. Strains up to 20% only: β = 0.21 ± 0.21, correlation −0.83.
Loading direction: refit step 3 with the data read as tension (λ = 1 + strain, |P|): c₁ = 12.97 kPa (+28.5%), χ²_ν = 20.7; over the first 5% only: +8.7% with χ²_ν = 0.38.

Plots: data with error bars, the 20% neo-Hookean fit and its extrapolation with band, the Gent fit (fig-01-25); normalised residuals for both models on all points (fig-01-26); the (c₁, β) confidence ellipses for the two ranges (fig-01-27).
expected_observations: Inside its range the neo-Hookean fit is clean and precise to 1%; outside it the prediction is 13% low, about eight times its own band: the interval measures noise, not model error.
Long runs of same-signed residuals and χ²_ν well above 1 reveal the wrong model once the data reach the strains where the models differ.
Linearised uncertainties agree with Monte Carlo for this well-conditioned fit; jointly fitted parameters are correlated, and β is undetermined by data that never exercise it.
The loading direction is part of the model: misreading it gives 28.5% error over 20% strain, and over a small range the residuals do not betray it.
extensions: Fit Mooney–Rivlin, P = 2(λ − λ⁻²)(c₁ + c₂/λ), which is linear in (c₁, c₂), and compare its 40% extrapolation with Gent's.
Experimental design: with 8 points, choose the stretches that minimise SE(β) and recompute; then argue from it where the next test should put its points.
Replace the σ_i by a single unknown σ estimated from the residuals and compare the parameter intervals.

exercises.prompt: Write down the five ingredients (data, model, loss, optimiser, evaluation) for (a) a linear trendline fitted in a spreadsheet to a strain-gauge calibration, gauge voltage against applied strain, and (b) a k-nearest-neighbour classifier (k = 5) that labels weld radiographs as acceptable or defective from 20 measured features. For (b), which ingredient is degenerate, and what does that imply about where its errors come from?
exercises.solution_sketch: (a) Data: (voltage, strain) pairs from one calibration run, with P the gauge's operating conditions (temperature, range). Model: strain = a + b·voltage, two parameters. Loss: squared error. Optimiser: closed form (normal equations). Evaluation: residuals at check points not used in the fit or on a second calibration run — the spreadsheet's R² is computed on the fitted points, i.e. training error. (b) Data: labelled radiographs from past inspections, P = welds of this type from this process. Model: majority vote of the 5 nearest stored examples in the 20-D feature space; its 'parameters' are the stored data, plus k and the distance. Loss: 0–1 loss, used only to choose k and the scaling by validation. Optimiser: none — training is storing the data; this is the degenerate ingredient. Evaluation: held-out welds split by weld or batch. Implication: everything rides on the data and the distance, so errors come from unrepresentative data, irrelevant features and unscaled distances, not from optimisation.

exercises.prompt: A linear model predicts tensile strength from material grade, one of {steel, aluminium, titanium}. (a) What does coding the grade as 1, 2, 3 assume? (b) You one-hot encode the grade into three columns and keep the column of ones for the intercept. Show that XᵀX is singular, and say what happens to the fitted weights and to the predictions. (c) Give two fixes.
exercises.solution_sketch: (a) That the effect is linear in the code: an order steel < aluminium < titanium and aluminium's effect exactly halfway between the other two. (b) The three one-hot columns sum to the column of ones in every row, so Xv = 0 for v = (−1, 1, 1, 1) over (intercept, steel, aluminium, titanium); then XᵀXv = 0 and XᵀX is singular. Any constant can be moved between the intercept and the three grade weights, so the weights are not unique; the predictions, being the projection of y onto the column space, are unique, and lstsq returns the minimum-norm weights. (c) Drop one grade column (a reference category) or drop the intercept; or add a ridge penalty, which makes XᵀX + λNI invertible.

exercises.prompt: The least-squares Hessian of a two-feature problem has eigenvalues 1 and 25. (a) What is the largest stable learning rate? (b) What is the best fixed learning rate, and the error contraction per step it gives? (c) How many steps reduce the error by a factor of 10⁶ at the best rate, and at η = 1/λ_max? (d) After standardisation the eigenvalues are 0.8 and 1.2. Repeat (b) and (c).

(a) Show that the gradient of binary cross-entropy with respect to the logit z is p̂ − y, where p̂ = σ(z). (b) Compute the gradient of ½(σ(z) − y)² with respect to z. (c) Evaluate both for a confidently wrong prediction, p̂ = 0.999 with y = 0, and for a confidently right one, p̂ = 0.001 with y = 0. (d) What do the numbers mean for learning?
exercises.solution_sketch: (a) ℓ = −y ln σ − (1 − y) ln(1 − σ) and dσ/dz = σ(1 − σ), so dℓ/dz = −y(1 − σ) + (1 − y)σ = σ − y. (b) (σ − y)σ(1 − σ). (c) Wrong: cross-entropy 0.999; squared error 0.999 × 0.999 × 0.001 = 0.000998, a ratio of about 1,001. Right: cross-entropy 0.001; squared error 0.001 × 0.001 × 0.999 ≈ 1.0×10⁻⁶. (d) Cross-entropy pushes in proportion to how wrong the model is; squared error through the sigmoid stops pushing exactly when the model is most wrong (saturation), so a confidently wrong model learns about a thousand times more slowly.

exercises.prompt: A crack detector has recall 0.90 and false-positive rate 0.03, and cracks are present in 2% of inspected parts. (a) What fraction of flagged parts actually have a crack, and how many false alarms come with each true one? (b) Show that the odds of a crack given an alarm are the prior odds times TPR/FPR, and use this to find the prevalence at which half the alarms are true. (c) Every flagged part goes to a second inspection with the same recall and false-positive rate, whose errors are independent of the first's given the true state. What fraction of twice-flagged parts have a crack, what is the recall of the two stages together, and what fraction of all parts does the second stage inspect? (d) Which numbers in the vendor's brochure would have hidden (a)?
exercises.solution_sketch: (a) Precision = 0.90 × 0.02/(0.90 × 0.02 + 0.03 × 0.98) = 0.0180/0.0474 = 0.380; each true alarm comes with 0.0294/0.0180 = 1.63 false ones. (b) By Bayes' rule, P(crack | alarm)/P(no crack | alarm) = TPR·π/(FPR·(1 − π)) = [π/(1 − π)]·(TPR/FPR): posterior odds are prior odds times the likelihood ratio, here 0.90/0.03 = 30. Half the alarms are true when the posterior odds are 1, i.e. π/(1 − π) = FPR/TPR, so π = FPR/(TPR + FPR) = 0.03/0.93 = 3.2%. Check on (a): 0.02/0.98 × 30 = 0.612, and 0.612/1.612 = 0.380. (c) The odds are multiplied by 30 again: 0.612 × 30 = 18.4, so 18.4/19.4 = 0.948 of twice-flagged parts have a crack; the recall is 0.90 × 0.90 = 0.81; the second stage inspects the 4.74% of parts the first flags. Independence is optimistic: two inspections that miss the same subtle cracks gain less. (d) Accuracy, 0.969, dominated by the 98% of good parts correctly passed, and ROC AUC, which does not depend on prevalence. Precision and the precision–recall curve at the real prevalence show what the inspectors will live with.

exercises.prompt: Six test parts receive scores. Defective: 0.9, 0.7, 0.4. Good: 0.8, 0.3, 0.2. (a) Compute the AUC by counting pairs. (b) Sweep the threshold downward and list the (FPR, TPR) points of the ROC curve; check that the area under the staircase equals (a). (c) At threshold 0.5, give precision and recall. (d) Which single score change would raise the AUC to 1?
exercises.solution_sketch: (a) Nine positive–negative pairs: 0.9 beats all three (3), 0.7 beats 0.3 and 0.2 (2), 0.4 beats 0.3 and 0.2 (2): AUC = 7/9 = 0.778. (b) (0, 0), (0, 1/3) at 0.9, (1/3, 1/3) at 0.8, (1/3, 2/3) at 0.7, (1/3, 1) at 0.4, (2/3, 1) at 0.3, (1, 1) at 0.2. Area = (1/3)(1/3) + (2/3)(1) = 7/9. (c) Flagged: 0.9, 0.8, 0.7; TP = 2, FP = 1, FN = 1: precision 2/3, recall 2/3. (d) Lower the good part scored 0.8 below 0.4 (for example to 0.35); raising 0.4 alone cannot work because 0.7 would still sit below 0.8.

exercises.prompt: You estimate a mean μ from n independent readings of variance σ², using the shrunk estimator μ̂_c = c·ȳ with 0 ≤ c ≤ 1. (a) Derive its bias², variance and mean squared error. (b) Find the c that minimises the MSE. (c) Take σ = 3 and n = 9. Evaluate c* and its MSE for μ = 2 and for μ = 0.5, and compare with the MSE of ȳ. (d) Why can you not use c* directly in practice? Compute the MSE when the c* for μ = 0.5 is used but μ is really 2, and say what this has to do with choosing λ by cross-validation.
exercises.solution_sketch: (a) E[cȳ] = cμ, so bias² = (1 − c)²μ²; Var = c²σ²/n; MSE = (1 − c)²μ² + c²σ²/n. (b) dMSE/dc = −2(1 − c)μ² + 2cσ²/n = 0 gives c* = μ²/(μ² + σ²/n). Then 1 − c* = (σ²/n)/(μ² + σ²/n), and substituting simplifies the minimum to MSE(c*) = μ²(σ²/n)/(μ² + σ²/n) = c*σ²/n. (c) σ²/n = 1, so ȳ has MSE 1.0. μ = 2: c* = 4/5 = 0.8, MSE 0.8 (bias² 0.16 + variance 0.64). μ = 0.5: c* = 0.25/1.25 = 0.2, MSE 0.2. Shrinking helps most when the signal is small against the noise. (d) c* depends on the unknown μ. Using c = 0.2 when μ = 2 gives 0.8² × 4 + 0.2² × 1 = 2.60, two and a half times the MSE of ȳ: shrinkage chosen without the data can do real harm. In practice the amount of shrinkage is chosen from data by validation or cross-validation, which estimates the error directly — exactly what Lab 3 does for λ.

exercises.prompt: (a) Derive the normal equations from the gradient of L(w) = (1/N)‖Xw − y‖². (b) Add the ridge penalty λ‖w‖² and show that the system becomes (XᵀX + λNI)w = Xᵀy. (c) Using the eigenvalues of XᵀX, explain why this system is solvable for every λ > 0, even when X has fewer rows than columns. (d) If XᵀX has eigenvalues 50 and 0.5 and λN = 5, give the shrinkage factor s²/(s² + λN) of each direction and the condition numbers before and after.
exercises.solution_sketch: (a) ∇L = (2/N)Xᵀ(Xw − y) = 0 gives XᵀXw = Xᵀy. (b) ∇(λ‖w‖²) = 2λw; (2/N)Xᵀ(Xw − y) + 2λw = 0; multiply by N/2: (XᵀX + λNI)w = Xᵀy. (c) XᵀX is symmetric with eigenvalues μ_i ≥ 0 because vᵀXᵀXv = ‖Xv‖² ≥ 0; adding λNI shifts each to μ_i + λN ≥ λN > 0, so every eigenvalue is positive and the matrix is invertible — including when N < d + 1 and some μ_i are zero. (d) 50/55 = 0.909 and 0.5/5.5 = 0.091: the well-determined direction keeps 91% of its least-squares value, the poorly determined one 9%; κ falls from 50/0.5 = 100 to 55/5.5 = 10.

exercises.prompt: For each set-up say whether there is leakage, of which kind, and how to fix it. (a) Missing values are imputed with the column mean of the full dataset, then 5-fold cross-validation is run. (b) Vibration spectra from 12 pumps, 500 per pump, are split 80/20 at random. (c) Next-day failure is predicted from features that include 'hours since last maintenance', recorded at the end of the day of the failure. (d) A model is tuned on the test set because the validation set was 'too small'.
exercises.solution_sketch: (a) Preprocessing leakage, usually mild: the means include validation rows. Impute inside a Pipeline fitted per fold. (b) Group leakage: each pump appears on both sides, so the model can recognise pumps. Split by pump (GroupKFold, for example leave two pumps out). (c) Target and temporal leakage: the maintenance after the failure resets the feature, so it encodes the label. Use only information available at prediction time, with an explicit time cut-off for every feature. (d) Test-set reuse: the test set has become a validation set and its number is optimistic. Tune by cross-validation on the training data and keep or collect an untouched test set.

exercises.prompt: A colleague reports 98% accuracy for a model that classifies hazards as controllable or not controllable. List the five questions you ask before believing it, and for each the answer that would make you trust the number.
exercises.solution_sketch: (1) What is the class balance, and what does the majority-class rule score? Trust if 98% is well above it. (2) What are the confusion matrix and the per-class precision and recall? Trust if the errors on the rare, costly class are acceptable. (3) How was the data split — by hazard scenario, system or project, or by row — and were duplicates removed? Trust if split by the unit that will be new in use. (4) How many models and settings were tried, and was the test set opened once after all choices? Trust if one look, recorded. (5) Do the test cases come from the conditions of use (same kinds of system, same labelling practice, recent), and how large is the test set? Trust if they do and the interval (for example from a bootstrap) is narrow. A sixth worth asking: how consistent are the human labels — agreement between labellers caps the accuracy that means anything.

exercises.prompt: You run a random search over 120 configurations of a gradient-boosting model, score each by 5-fold cross-validation and report the best score. (a) Why is that score optimistic even if every configuration is equally good? (b) Does the optimism grow or shrink with (i) more configurations, (ii) more data, (iii) configurations so alike that their scores are nearly identical? One sentence each. (c) What is the remedy, and why does it work?
exercises.solution_sketch: (a) Each cross-validation score is the configuration's true performance plus noise from the particular folds. Picking the largest picks the configuration whose noise happened to be most favourable, so the maximum is biased upward even when no configuration is better than another (Section 10). (b) (i) Grows, but slowly: the expected maximum of n independent noisy scores rises roughly like √(ln n) standard errors. (ii) Shrinks: each score's standard error falls like 1/√N, and the optimism with it. (iii) Shrinks: strongly correlated scores behave like fewer independent draws, so there is less to select from. (c) Nested cross-validation, or a test set opened once after every choice is made: the chosen model is scored on data the selection never saw, so the selection's luck is not counted. Lab 4's extension shows the size of the effect on pure noise.

exercises.prompt: A k-nearest-neighbour classifier (k = 5, standardised features) detects bearing faults well from 3 vibration features computed on about 3,000 labelled windows. A new data logger adds 47 further features, most of them unrelated to faults, and the cross-validated accuracy falls although no information was removed. (a) Give two reasons, both about distances. (b) Name two remedies. (c) Why would a gradient-boosted tree ensemble lose much less from the same 47 features?
exercises.solution_sketch: (a) After standardisation each irrelevant feature contributes as much to the squared distance as each informative one, so 47 noise terms swamp 3 signal terms and the 'nearest' neighbours are near in irrelevant directions. And the curse of dimensionality: in 50 dimensions a neighbourhood holding a fixed fraction of the data spans most of every feature's range (Section 11's sub-cube calculation), so the 5 nearest of a few thousand points are not local at all. (b) Select features by validation, inside the folds so as not to repeat Lab 4's leak; reduce d with PCA or domain knowledge; or learn a weighted distance. (c) Each split of a tree uses one feature, chosen for the impurity reduction it buys, so irrelevant features are seldom chosen and no distance ever mixes all 50 of them.

exercises.prompt: Test the claim that gradient boosting is the baseline to beat on tabular data. With 5-fold cross-validation using the same folds for every model (KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)), compare the RMSE of: predicting the mean (DummyRegressor); ridge (StandardScaler + RidgeCV(alphas=np.logspace(−3, 3, 13))); k-NN (StandardScaler + KNeighborsRegressor(10)); an RBF support-vector regressor (StandardScaler + SVR(C=10)); a random forest (300 trees, random_state=0); and HistGradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=0), on (a) make_friedman1(n_samples=2000, n_features=10, noise=1.0, random_state=0) and (b) load_diabetes. Report mean ± standard deviation over folds and the fit time. Then compute the fold-wise RMSE differences between the two best models on each dataset and say whether the ranking is supported.
exercises.solution_sketch: Friedman #1 (2,000 rows, 5 informative features with an interaction and a nonlinearity, 5 irrelevant): mean 5.02 ± 0.09, ridge 2.59 ± 0.09, k-NN 2.52 ± 0.07, random forest 1.79 ± 0.07, SVR 1.40 ± 0.05, boosting 1.34 ± 0.04. SVR minus boosting per fold: 0.092, 0.094, 0.025, 0.014, 0.072 (mean 0.059, SD 0.038): boosting wins in all five folds. Diabetes (442 rows, nearly additive signal): mean 76.9 ± 4.5, ridge 54.6 ± 2.2, SVR 55.6 ± 2.8, k-NN 56.8 ± 3.0, forest 57.8 ± 4.1, boosting 59.0 ± 5.5. SVR minus ridge: 0.11, 0.76, −1.92, 4.79, 1.18 (mean 0.99, SD 2.44) — no supported difference; boosting minus ridge has mean 4.37 with ridge better in four folds of five. Conclusion: boosting wins when the target has interactions and nonlinearity and there are enough rows; on a few hundred rows with an additive signal, a linear model is as good or better. Run the ladder rather than assume, and judge differences fold by fold. The whole script runs in well under a minute (if HistGradientBoosting is unexpectedly slow, limit OpenMP threads with OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 or 2).

exercises.prompt: In Lab 5's neo-Hookean fit over strains up to 20%, change the point at λ = 0.90 from −6.98 kPa to −8.00 kPa. (a) Refit with its recorded σ = 0.185 kPa: how far does c₁ move, what is that point's normalised residual, and what happens to χ²_ν? (b) Refit with that point's σ multiplied by ten. (c) Which behaviour do you want, and what does this say about recording uncertainties?
exercises.solution_sketch: (a) c₁ moves from 10.09 to 10.29 kPa (+2%, two standard deviations); the point's normalised residual is −6.0; χ²_ν rises from 0.71 to 6.4. The fit is pulled, but the diagnostics flag the point. (b) c₁ = 10.05 kPa, residual −0.7, χ²_ν = 0.54: the point is effectively ignored. (c) If the reading really was that precise, (a) is right and the specimen or the model needs explaining; if a problem was known (slip at the platen, a bubble), a large σ is the honest record. The σ_i are part of the data: a wrong small σ lets one bad point move the answer, and a missing σ makes the check impossible — which is why the fit refuses points without one.

exercises.prompt: A colleague exports a compression test with the stretches written as 1 + strain and the stresses as positive numbers, and fits the neo-Hookean model with the loading direction declared as tension. (a) Which of Lab 5's input checks fire, and why can no input check catch this mistake? (b) Over the first 5% of strain the misread fit looks clean; over 20% it does not. Explain from the way g(λ) = λ − λ⁻² bends on either side of λ = 1, without computing. (c) What must be stored with the fitted c₁ so that the next user cannot repeat the mistake?
exercises.solution_sketch: (a) None. Stretches above 1 with positive stresses form a self-consistent tension test, and checks catch only contradictions — a stretch on the wrong side of 1 for the declared direction, a stress of the wrong sign, a missing σ — not a consistent mislabel; only the test record (the platens moved together) can. (b) g has the same slope on both sides of λ = 1 and bends downward, so |g| grows faster than linearly in compression and slower than linearly in tension. To first order in the strain the two branches agree, and misread data look like a slightly stiffer tension test with a clean fit; the second-order difference grows with the strain until it exceeds the noise and the residuals show runs (Section 12: +8.7% with χ²_ν = 0.38 over 5%; +28.5% with χ²_ν = 20.7 over 20%). (c) The loading direction and the strain range fitted over, with the residual diagnostics: the coefficient means something only for the test it came from.

quiz.question: The normal equations Xᵀ(y − Xw) = 0 say that, at the least-squares solution,
options: the residual vector is orthogonal to every column of X
the weight vector is orthogonal to y
quiz.explanation: Xᵀr = 0 means each column of X has zero inner product with the residual r: ŷ is the orthogonal projection of y onto the column space. The residuals are zero only if y lies in that space; nothing makes w orthogonal to y; XᵀX is the identity only for orthonormal columns.

quiz.question: Gradient descent runs on L(w) = ½wᵀHw where H has eigenvalues 0.5 and 8. Which learning rate diverges?
quiz.explanation: Stability needs η < 2/λ_max = 2/8 = 0.25. At 0.26 the steep mode's factor is 1 − 0.26·8 = −1.08, so it grows. 0.24 still converges, oscillating (factor −0.92); 0.10 and 0.20 converge.

quiz.question: Two centred, uncorrelated features have standard deviations 1 and 100. The condition number of XᵀX/N is about
quiz.explanation: XᵀX/N = diag(1², 100²), so κ = 10⁴ = (ratio of standard deviations)². 100 is the ratio itself, not squared; the other values have no basis.

quiz.question: Constant-step SGD has reached its noise floor near a minimum. Halving the learning rate will, approximately,
options: halve the stationary excess loss and slow the approach
make the iterate converge exactly to the minimum
quiz.explanation: The stationary variance is ηs²/(Bλ(2 − ηλ)) ≈ ηs²/(2Bλ), proportional to η. The floor halves but never reaches zero; exact convergence needs a step that decays (Robbins–Monro) or a growing batch.

quiz.question: If the noise in y follows a Laplace distribution, maximum likelihood fits the model with which loss, and what is the best constant prediction?
quiz.explanation: The Laplace negative log-likelihood is |y − f(x)|/b plus a constant, so the loss is absolute error, whose best constant is the median. Squared error and the mean belong to Gaussian noise; cross-entropy belongs to Bernoulli or categorical outcomes.

quiz.question: For binary cross-entropy with p̂ = σ(z), the derivative of the loss with respect to the logit z is
quiz.explanation: The sigmoid's derivative cancels against the logarithm, leaving p̂ − y, which is large when the model is confidently wrong. (p̂ − y)p̂(1 − p̂) is the gradient of ½(p̂ − y)², which vanishes in that case; y − p̂ has the wrong sign; −log p̂ is the loss itself for y = 1.

quiz.question: A test has recall 0.8 and false-positive rate 0.01. The condition it detects has prevalence 0.2%. The fraction of positive results that are true is about
quiz.explanation: Precision = 0.8·0.002/(0.8·0.002 + 0.01·0.998) = 0.0016/0.0116 = 0.14. False alarms outnumber true detections about six to one because negatives are 499 times more common.

quiz.question: A degree-15 polynomial fitted to 20 noisy points has training RMSE 0.11 and validation RMSE 0.72, against a noise level of 0.3. Which term of the bias–variance decomposition dominates its validation error?
options: None: the decomposition only holds for linear models
quiz.explanation: The flexible model follows the noise of its particular training set, so its predictions change a great deal from sample to sample: variance (0.87 of the expected 0.96 in Section 8). Its bias² is near zero. The noise contributes 0.09 whatever the model. The decomposition holds for any model under squared error.

quiz.question: Ridge regression is the MAP estimate under which prior on the weights?
options: No prior: ridge is a maximum-likelihood estimate
quiz.explanation: A Gaussian prior adds ‖w‖²/(2τ²) to the negative log-posterior, giving λ = σ²/(Nτ²). The Laplace prior gives the lasso's L1 penalty; a uniform prior gives back maximum likelihood; ridge is not maximum likelihood because of the penalty.

quiz.question: Which of these is NOT leakage?
options: Fitting a StandardScaler on the training folds only, inside a Pipeline
Selecting the 20 most correlated features on all the data, then cross-validating
Splitting repeated measurements of the same specimens by row
Shuffling a time series before cross-validation
quiz.explanation: Preprocessing fitted only on training folds sees no validation data. The other three let information from the validation data or the future into training: selection on all data (Lab 4: 0.87 on noise), group leakage, temporal leakage.

quiz.question: For which model would rescaling one feature from millimetres to metres leave the fitted predictions unchanged?
quiz.explanation: Trees split on one feature at a time by thresholds, which move with the rescaling, so the partitions and predictions are unchanged. k-NN and RBF kernels use distances that mix the units; ridge penalises coefficients whose size depends on the units.

quiz.question: A neo-Hookean fit over 0–20% strain has a 95% interval of ±1% on c₁, yet its prediction at 40% strain is 13% low. The best explanation is
options: The interval quantifies noise assuming the model is right; it does not include model error outside the fitted range
More data inside 0–20% would fix the extrapolation
The noise is larger at 40% strain
quiz.explanation: Lab 5's interval agrees with Monte Carlo, so it is not wrong; it is conditional on the model. The material stiffens beyond 20% (it is a Gent solid), which no amount of small-strain data can reveal. Larger noise would widen the band, not bias the prediction by 13%.

papers.citation: Belkin, M., Hsu, D., Ma, S., Mandal, S. “Reconciling modern machine-learning practice and the classical bias–variance trade-off.” Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), 2019.
papers.why: The paper that named double descent. It shows where the classical U-shaped validation curve of Section 8 stops being the whole story, and why the decomposition itself still holds.
papers.read: Read the abstract, the introduction up to and including Figure 1, and the section on random Fourier features with its figure. Skip the theoretical analysis and the supplementary material.
questions: What is the interpolation threshold, and where does it sit for random Fourier features?
Beyond the threshold many parameter vectors fit the training data exactly. Which one do the authors choose, and why does that choice matter for test error?
Does double descent contradict the bias–variance decomposition you derived in Section 8? Explain in two sentences.
What does the paper imply for choosing model size by validation in practice?

papers.citation: Kapoor, S., Narayanan, A. “Leakage and the reproducibility crisis in machine-learning-based science.” Patterns, 2023.
papers.why: A survey of leakage in published machine-learning-based science, with a taxonomy that turns Lab 4's three cases into a checklist, and a case study in which a celebrated advantage of complex models disappears once leakage is fixed.
papers.read: Read the introduction, the leakage taxonomy (its table and the definition of each type) and the civil-war prediction case study. Skim the field-by-field survey and the model info sheet.
questions: Place each of Lab 4's three leaky pipelines in the paper's taxonomy.
What happened to the reported advantage of complex models over logistic regression in the civil-war case once the errors were corrected?
Which items of the authors' proposed documentation (model info sheets) would have caught the group leak in Lab 4?
Name one type of leakage in the taxonomy that a test set opened only once does not protect against, and say why.

papers.citation: Domingos, P. “A few useful things to know about machine learning.” Communications of the ACM, 2012.
papers.why: A practitioner's summary of lessons this module derives formally; reading it last tests whether the formal versions stuck, and it is the article to hand a colleague who asks what this module was about.
papers.read: Read the sections on learning as representation plus evaluation plus optimisation, on generalisation, on overfitting (with the dartboard figure), on intuition failing in high dimensions, and on more data beating a cleverer algorithm. Skim the rest.
questions: Domingos splits a learner into representation, evaluation and optimisation. Map these onto the five ingredients of Section 1. Which ingredients does he leave implicit?
Which of his four dartboards corresponds to the unregularised degree-15 polynomial on 20 points in Lab 3, and which to the degree-1 fit?
He says more data beats a cleverer algorithm. Using the learning curves of Section 8, say when that is true and when it is false.
Which of his high-dimensional intuitions does Section 11's sub-cube calculation quantify, and which does the k-NN scenario of exercise e12 illustrate?

widgets.name: gd-quadratic
widgets.teaching_point: The learning rate is capped by the steepest direction (η < 2/λ_max) while the speed is set by the flattest (factor 1 − ηλ_min per step), so the number of steps grows with the condition number; with gradient noise a constant step stalls at a floor proportional to η.
controls: slider: learning rate η from 0.01 to 2.5, logarithmic, default 1.8 (λ_max is fixed at 1, so η is read in units of 1/λ_max; tick marks at 1 and 2)
slider: condition number κ from 1 to 1000, logarithmic, default 20 (λ_min = 1/κ)
slider: gradient noise σ_g from 0 to 1, linear, default 0 (0 is full-batch gradient descent; used again in Section 4)
buttons: Step (one iteration), Run/Pause (10 iterations per second, up to 300), Reset
click on the contour plot: sets the starting point

dropdown of presets: 'well conditioned (κ = 1, η = 1)', 'standardised but correlated, ρ = 0.8 (κ = 9)', 'units differ tenfold (κ = 100)', 'units differ thirtyfold (κ = 900)', 'zig-zag (κ = 20, η = 1.8)', 'just unstable (κ = 20, η = 2.05)'
displays: contour plot of the loss over [−4, 4]² with equal axis scales: 12 level sets drawn analytically as ellipses (semi-axes √(2c/λ_max) and √(2c/λ_min) along the eigenvectors, levels c log-spaced from 10⁻³ to 10), eigen-directions as faint dashed lines, the minimum at the origin, and the iterates joined by a polyline with dots

loss against iteration on a log axis from 10⁻¹² to 10³, with the envelope L₀ρ^(2t), ρ = max(|1 − η|, |1 − η/κ|), dashed; when σ_g > 0 a horizontal dashed line at the predicted floor Σ_i ησ_g²/(2(2 − ηλ_i))
two bars showing |1 − ηλ_max| and |1 − ηλ_min| against a red line at 1

readouts: λ_max = 1, λ_min, κ, η, the two factors, status ('converging', 'oscillating across the valley', 'marginal', 'diverged at step t'), predicted steps for a 10⁶ loss reduction from the envelope, and actual steps
widgets.defaults: κ = 20, η = 1.8, σ_g = 0, start at −3.5 along the flat eigenvector plus 1.5 along the steep one (w₀ ≈ (−3.78, −0.45), L₀ = 1.431). The path zig-zags across the valley (steep factor −0.8) while creeping along it (flat factor 0.91); the loss falls by 10⁶ in 66 steps against an envelope prediction of 73.
widgets.spec: Loss L(w) = ½(λ_max(v_maxᵀw)² + λ_min(v_minᵀw)²) with λ_max = 1, λ_min = 1/κ, v_min = (cos 30°, sin 30°) (the valley direction), v_max = (−sin 30°, cos 30°); minimum at the origin. Update w ← w − η(Hw + σ_g ξ) with ξ two independent standard normals from a seeded generator (mulberry32 with seed 1, Box–Muller), reseeded on Reset so runs are repeatable. Stop and report 'diverged at step t' when L > 10⁶ or ‖w‖ > 10³; report 'converged in t steps' when σ_g = 0 and L < 10⁻⁶·L₀; at exactly η = 2 report 'marginal: the steep mode neither grows nor decays'. With σ_g > 0 run to 300 steps and show the running mean of L over the last 100 steps next to the predicted floor. Predicted steps = 6 ln 10/(−2 ln ρ) when ρ < 1, '1' when ρ = 0, '∞' when ρ ≥ 1, printed with thousands separators (κ = 1000 at η = 0.01 predicts 690,772). Reference values for testing, from the default start: κ = 1, η = 1 converges in 1 step; κ = 1, η = 1.8 in 31; κ = 20, η = 1.0 in 120; κ = 20, η = 0.5 in 243; κ = 100, η = 1.8 in 299; κ = 1000, η = 1.8 in 2,386; κ = 20, η = 2.05 diverges at step 141. With σ_g = 0.3 and κ = 20 the floor is 0.0681 at η = 1.0, 0.0264 at η = 0.5 and 0.0046 at η = 0.1 (simulation agrees to three figures). Vanilla JavaScript and SVG, no libraries; native range inputs with labels so the widget works from the keyboard; colours from the page's CSS variables so both light and dark themes work; all strings in one object for the Chinese translation.

widgets.name: polynomial-capacity
widgets.teaching_point: Training error falls with every degree added, while validation error is U-shaped because bias² falls and variance rises; more data shrinks the variance and moves the best degree to the right.
controls: slider: polynomial degree from 0 to 15, integer, default 3 (capped at N − 1)
segmented buttons: number of training points N = 10, 20, 50 or 200, default 20
slider: noise σ from 0.05 to 0.6, default 0.3
button: 'new noise draw' (advances the training-noise seed)
checkbox: 'show bias² and variance', default on
displays: left: training points as filled dots, 60 of the validation points as hollow dots, the true function sin(2πx) dashed and the fitted polynomial solid; y-axis clipped to [−2.5, 2.5] with a small marker where the curve leaves the range
right top: training and validation RMSE against degree 0–15 on a log axis from 0.01 to 10, a vertical line at the current degree, a dashed horizontal line at σ
right bottom (when checked): bias², variance, σ² and their sum against degree on a log axis, from exact formulas, with the minimum of the sum marked
readouts: current training and validation RMSE, best degree on validation, best degree by expected error
widgets.defaults: N = 20, σ = 0.3, degree 3, noise seed 0: the cubic follows the sine. Dragging to degree 15 sends the training RMSE to about 0.1 and the validation RMSE to about 0.7; switching to N = 200 flattens the right-hand side.
widgets.spec: Fixed design x_i = i/(N − 1), i = 0..N − 1; y_i = sin(2πx_i) + σε_i with ε_i standard normals from mulberry32(seed) and Box–Muller. Validation set: 500 points with x uniform on [0, 1] and their own normals from a fixed seed (12345), scaled by the current σ. Features: Legendre polynomials P_0..P_d of t = 2x − 1 by the recurrence (k + 1)P_(k+1) = (2k + 1)tP_k − kP_(k−1). Fit by least squares with a Householder QR of the N × (d + 1) design — never the normal equations of a monomial basis. Bias and variance exactly, for the fixed design: on a grid of 201 points x_g, the smoother matrix S = Φ_g R⁻¹Qᵀ gives bias²(x_g) = ((S f)_g − f(x_g))² with f the true function at the training x, and variance(x_g) = σ² Σ_j S_gj²; average both over the grid; expected test MSE = mean bias² + mean variance + σ². Recompute all degrees when N, σ or the seed changes (at most 16 QR factorisations of a 200 × 16 matrix). Degrees ≥ N are disabled; at d = N − 1 the fit interpolates and the training RMSE is 0, shown as 'interpolates'. The random draws differ from Lab 3's NumPy draws, but the exact curves are deterministic and must match Lab 3's table for N = 20, σ = 0.3: degree 3 bias² 0.0052 and variance 0.0161 (sum with σ² 0.1113, the minimum); degree 9 variance 0.0422; degree 15 variance 0.8737; for N = 200 the minimum moves to degree 5 (0.0927). Vanilla JavaScript and SVG, keyboard-operable controls, theme colours from CSS variables, strings in one object for translation.

NOTATION. L(θ) is the MEAN loss (1/N)Σℓ everywhere. Least squares: H = (2/N)XᵀX, stability η < 2/λ_max(H), condition number κ = λ_max/λ_min. Ridge adds λ‖w‖² to the mean loss, giving (XᵀX + λNI)w = Xᵀy; MAP gives λ = σ²/(Nτ²); lasso adds λ‖w‖₁ and soft-thresholds at λ/2 for XᵀX = NI. Library mapping: Ridge α = λN, Lasso α = λ/2, LogisticRegression C = 1/(2Nλ). Use ½(p̂ − y)² for the squared-error-through-sigmoid comparison so its gradient is (p̂ − y)p̂(1 − p̂). λ has three jobs: eigenvalues (λ_i, λ_max, λ_min) in Sections 3–4, regularisation strength in Section 9 (write the eigenvalues of XᵀX there as s_i²), stretch in Section 12 (say so in that section). B is the mini-batch size only (BRIEF): the number of bootstrap replicates is R (as are Lab 3's Monte Carlo draws), the number of trees in a forest or boosted ensemble is M, and McNemar's discordant counts are n₁₀ (A right, B wrong) and n₀₁ (A wrong, B right), because b is already the intercept and the Laplace scale. The Gent parameter is β = 1/J_m; neo-Hookean is β = 0; μ = 2c₁ and E = 6c₁. Use Unicode-light LaTeX consistent with 00-README: bold lower-case vectors, bold upper-case matrices, natural logarithms.

DEPARTURES FROM THE EDITOR'S SUGGESTIONS, AND WHY. (a) SGD (Section 4) comes straight after gradient descent on the quadratic, so Lab 1 covers closed form, GD and SGD after its own reading; the stability bound is derived in Section 3, where the quadratic is. (b) Metrics (Section 7) follow logistic regression directly, so Lab 2 measures what it builds; basic k-fold cross-validation sits in Section 8 so Lab 3 can use it; nested CV, leakage and bootstrap intervals are Section 10. Consequently the editor's labs 2 and 3 are swapped: Lab 2 is logistic regression with metrics, Lab 3 is polynomials. (c) The engineering case generates its data from a Gent material, so the neo-Hookean fit is clean in range and visibly wrong beyond it; this makes residual analysis and extrapolation risk measurable, and the Gent fit makes nonlinear least squares necessary (the neo-Hookean model alone is linear in c₁). (d) The claim that gradient boosting is the baseline to beat is tested in exercise e13, which includes a dataset (load_diabetes) where ridge wins; do not state the claim without that qualification. (e) The probability refresher opens Section 5, where likelihoods first appear; Section 2 introduces least squares geometrically.

TRAPS. scikit-learn's breast-cancer target codes malignant as 0: flip it. LogisticRegression's default tol=1e-4 leaves coefficient differences of 0.016 against a converged NumPy solution; use tol=1e-8 when comparing. For logistic regression the bound η < 2/L is sufficient, not necessary (η = 5 still works); do not present it as exact. Use the Legendre basis legvander(2x − 1, d): with standardised monomials even α = 1e-10 already regularises, so the ridge path never shows its overfitting end. The Monte Carlo bias² is inflated by variance/R (0.005 at degree 15 with R = 200); say so where Lab 3 compares it with the exact values. R² on forward-chaining folds can be negative; prefer RMSE when comparing splitting schemes. On the build machine HistGradientBoosting slowed a hundredfold under OpenMP contention; one fit normally takes about 0.1 s, so if it is slow, set OMP_NUM_THREADS to 1 or 2. Double descent is a phenomenon under specific conditions (interpolating fits, minimum-norm solutions), not a law; the U-shaped curve remains the default expectation for classical models. McNemar's χ² form (n₁₀ − n₀₁)²/(n₁₀ + n₀₁) overstates the evidence at moderate counts (24 against 12 gives p = 0.046 against an exact 0.065): compute the exact test with scipy.stats.binomtest and present the χ² form only as the large-count approximation.
